"question-621a7d94-aa15-5da2-a86e-6e37bead83f1" :question/id #uuid "621a7d94-aa15-5da2-a86e-6e37bead83f1" :question/math-academy-id "q-123585" :question/problem "Find the value of $\operatorname{sec}⁡({180}^{∘})+\operatorname{csc}⁡({90}^{∘}).$" :question/worked-solution "The angles ${180}^{∘}$ and ${90}^{∘}$ are quadrantal angles. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](images/79/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

- Let's first consider the angle ${180}^{∘}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle ${180}^{∘}$ corresponds to the point $(-1,0).$  Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}⁡({180}^{∘})=-1.$ Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡({180}^{∘})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡({180}^{∘})}=\frac{1}{-1}=-1.
$$

- Now, let's consider the angle ${90}^{∘}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle ${90}^{∘}$ corresponds to the point $(0,1).$  Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}⁡({90}^{∘})=1.$ Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡({90}^{∘})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡({90}^{∘})}=\frac{1}{1}=1.
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡({180}^{∘})+\operatorname{csc}⁡({90}^{∘})=-1+1=0.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-99de1166-6614-59dc-ba88-9b3adbcbf5e8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-99de1166-6614-59dc-ba88-9b3adbcbf5e8" :answer-field/id #uuid "99de1166-6614-59dc-ba88-9b3adbcbf5e8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-16e33752-dbec-5be0-abda-0b23cc352083" :answer-field/choices ["answer-65a2005c-6f9c-5b3b-92b5-b91a280aa805" "answer-7ac225ab-a108-5cf1-b663-e25ab4138d7b" "answer-16e33752-dbec-5be0-abda-0b23cc352083" "answer-fc8fae09-f797-5025-b37c-64365f7ed7cd" "answer-80712ae4-c0c2-56af-a31a-939b00f59f46"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-65a2005c-6f9c-5b3b-92b5-b91a280aa805" :answer/id #uuid "65a2005c-6f9c-5b3b-92b5-b91a280aa805" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7ac225ab-a108-5cf1-b663-e25ab4138d7b" :answer/id #uuid "7ac225ab-a108-5cf1-b663-e25ab4138d7b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-16e33752-dbec-5be0-abda-0b23cc352083" :answer/id #uuid "16e33752-dbec-5be0-abda-0b23cc352083" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fc8fae09-f797-5025-b37c-64365f7ed7cd" :answer/id #uuid "fc8fae09-f797-5025-b37c-64365f7ed7cd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-80712ae4-c0c2-56af-a31a-939b00f59f46" :answer/id #uuid "80712ae4-c0c2-56af-a31a-939b00f59f46" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "Undefined" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-5dc0c374-75b0-5038-a236-6349d3712634" :question/id #uuid "5dc0c374-75b0-5038-a236-6349d3712634" :question/math-academy-id "q-23418" :question/problem "Find the value of $\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}).$" :question/worked-solution "The angle $\frac{\pi }{2}$ is a quadrantal angle. The unit circle below illustrates the quadrantal angles that lie on the range $[0^\circ, 360^\circ).$

![](images/79/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

We can identify four points on the unit circle above,

$$
(1,0), \quad (0,1), \quad (-1,0), \quad (0,-1),
$$

that correspond to the angles

$$
0^\circ, \quad 90^\circ,\quad 180^\circ, \quad 270^\circ,
$$

in degrees, or

$$
0, \quad \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \quad \pi, \quad \dfrac{3\pi}{2},
$$

in radians.

We can use these points to find cosine and sine of quadrantal angles. First, recall that a point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta$ using the following formulas:

$$
x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta
$$

For example, if we are asked to find the value of $\cos(\pi),$ then we just look at the $\color{blue}x$-coordinate of the corresponding point. The point is $({\color{blue}{-1}},0),$ and therefore, we get

$$
\cos(\pi)={\color{blue}{-1}}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059944 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186204024 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-272bf8c6-2369-5e98-9adb-ebe6db7bece2" "question-cd16fbf2-f5ff-5242-b610-fb61c79ec2b3" "question-08790f4f-fd5e-5556-9203-49eaf6e8edd8" "question-5830491e-19ce-53b6-8fb0-b5e123e740a5"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-272bf8c6-2369-5e98-9adb-ebe6db7bece2" :question/id #uuid "272bf8c6-2369-5e98-9adb-ebe6db7bece2" :question/math-academy-id "q-257192" :question/problem "Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-2,2]\times [0,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where

$$
f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x.
$$

Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[-1,\,0]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).

<table align="center" cellpadding="1" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" rowspan="2">${x}_{1}≈[$</td>
<td align="center" height="25" width="25">
$0.348$
</td>
<td align="center" rowspan="2">$]$</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" height="25" width="25">
{{field-1}}
</td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}y-x\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}y-x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y-x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{y}^{2}+6 & 8xy-1 \\ 8xy-1 & 4{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$

$$
{H}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-∇f({x}_{n}).

$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-y+1) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(-4xy-x-1) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-y+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(-4xy-x-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6x & -4y-1 \\ -4y-1 & -4x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}6x & -4y-1 \\ -4y-1 & -4x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-y+1 \\ -4xy-x-1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.

$$

$$

{\begin{bmatrix}4y & 4x \\ 4x & -4\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{\begin{bmatrix}4xy-4 \\ 2{x}^{2}-2-4y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.

$$

Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system." :question/worked-solution "The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & -8 & 4 \\ -4 & 8 & -4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using the standard Gauss-Jordan method, we can reduce this matrix to reduced row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & -8 & 4 \\ -4 & 8 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & -8 & 4 \\ -4 & 8 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 8 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now  

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and we have one free variable, $y.$ That means we need to find $x$  in terms of $y.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=2y+1 \\ y &=y,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $y$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2y+1 \\ y\end{bmatrix},\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5be30950-b64e-577a-ae02-66dc69074ea6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "q-131714" :question/problem "Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y+z &=4 \\ y-3z &=-1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system." :question/worked-solution "The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using the standard Gauss-Jordan method, we can reduce this matrix to reduced row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -5 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now  

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-5z &=2 \\ y-3z &=-1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are $x$ and $y,$ and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=5z+2 \\ y &=3z-1 \\ z &=z,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $z$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5z+2 \\ 3z-1 \\ z\end{bmatrix},\,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-38a28058-8837-5c47-bd4f-999f7f79529b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id of equations.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-x+y &=-1 \\ 2x+3y &=3 \\ -x-4y &=-3.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. The system is inconsistent

II. The system has a unique solution

III. The system is consistent dependent" :question/worked-solution "To classify the system, we first need to find its solution. The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 & 3 \\ -1 & -4 & -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using the method of Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 & 3 \\ -1 & -4 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 \\ -1 & -4 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & -5 & -2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The final row corresponds to the equation $0x+0y=-1,$ and this has no solution. Therefore, our system has no solution, and we conclude that the system is inconsistent.

As a result, only statement I is true." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-eda18abf-1e9e-51ea-a1af-55bc7948bea6"] :db/ensure "fcf32a74-971a-505b-b459-ef18eedf0a90" :question/math-academy-id "q-143715" :question/problem "Consider the polar curve $r={cos}^{2}⁡\theta$ for $\theta \in [0,\pi ).$ Given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ),
$$

and ${x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0$

II. ${lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=0$

III. The curve has a horizontal tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$

*Hint: It is not necessary to use L'Hopital's rule to evaluate the limit in part II.*" :question/worked-solution "When a polar curve is differentiable at a point ${\theta }_{0}$, there is a horizontal tangent at ${\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}=0
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative ${y}^{′}(x)$ takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a horizontal tangent at this point if

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=0.
$$

In this case, we're told that ${x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${y}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})({cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Computing the limit as $\theta \to \frac{\pi }{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta ){cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}(\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta ){cos}^{\cancel{2}}⁡(\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}) \\  & =\frac{0-2\cdot 1}{-3\cdot 1\cdot 0} \\  & =\frac{-2}{0} \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the limit in part II does *not* equal to $0,$ there curve does *not* have a horizontal tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}.$ In fact, it is a vertical tangent.

![](images/f4/f4609e6433a861ef255cbeeac60c8a316e5c14a89df45030e26e526e3a1253a4.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e16e2010-e951-50c2-8dc9-1ddcbae83f31"] :db/ensure II. ${lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=0$

*Hint: It is not necessary to use L'Hopital's rule to evaluate the limit in part II.*" :question/worked-solution "When a polar curve is differentiable at a point ${\theta }_{0}$, there is a horizontal tangent at ${\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}=0
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative ${y}^{′}(x)$ takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a horizontal tangent at this point if

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=0.
$$

In this case, we're told that ${x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Substituting $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${y}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =3{sin}^{2}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Computing the limit as $\theta \to \frac{\pi }{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}(\frac{3{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{3}⁡\theta \,(3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2)}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}(\frac{12{sin}^{2}⁡(\theta ){cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{3}⁡\theta \,(3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2)}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}(\frac{12{sin}^{\cancel{2}}⁡(\theta ){\cancel{cos}}^{2}(\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{8\cancel{sin}\theta {cos}^{\cancel{3}}⁡\theta \,(3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2)}) \\  & =\frac{12\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,(3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2)} \\  & =\frac{12\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})}{8\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})(3{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-2)} \\  & =\frac{12\cdot 1\cdot (-1)}{0\cdot (3\cdot 0-2)} \\  & =\frac{-12}{0} \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the limit in part II does *not* equal to $0,$ there curve does *not* have a horizontal tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}.$ In fact, it is a vertical tangent.

![](images/32/32a586a1fe160a6c3a2cfee3cfb78af3d596679cf40abedeb0b8d622a3cf736c.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4b4c2f95-49e5-5e7b-9fbf-f50c23d0825b"] $$

$$

$$

$$

$$

{:db/id "question-1355c292-a399-578d-8bac-2939b3befda0" :question/id #uuid "1355c292-a399-578d-8bac-2939b3befda0" :question/math-academy-id "q-145039" :question/problem "Consider the polar curve $r={cos}^{2}⁡\theta$ for $\theta \in [0,\pi ).$ Given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ),
$$

and ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0$

II. ${lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\infty$

III. The curve has a vertical tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$" :question/worked-solution "For a given polar curve, there is a vertical tangent at $\theta ={\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a vertical tangent at this point if

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty \,\text{and}\,{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty .
$$

In this case, we're told that ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${x}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}){cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-3\cdot 1\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Computing the limit as $\theta \to {(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{+},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta }) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{\cancel{cos}\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{\cancel{2}}⁡\theta }) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}) \\  & =\frac{0-2\cdot 1}{-3\cdot 1\cdot {0}^{-}} \\  & =\frac{-2}{{0}^{+}} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Using the calculations from part II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}) \\  & =\frac{0-2\cdot 1}{-3\cdot 1\cdot {0}^{+}} \\  & =\frac{-2}{{0}^{-}} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Since the limits of our derivative are both infinite, there is a vertical tangent to the curve at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}.$

![](images/50/50637a502a56fc242ba5d8e2fda59ddc899295d4b14f7ae692869536b95ef661.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fce87f54-6287-5426-bb0b-5253c4ba2656"] :db/ensure "9cdf7c4f-4409-57f0-b1eb-dca5de834f65" :question/math-academy-id "q-276297" :question/problem "A fair spinner has six sides labeled with the numbers $-2,$ $-1,$ $0,$ $1,$ $2,$ and $3.$ If the spinner is spun, what is the expected value of the outcome?

$\text{E}[X]=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x).
$$

Let $X$ be the outcome of the spinner. Then the support is $S=\{-2,-1,0,1,2,3\},$ and the corresponding probabilities are all $\frac{1}{6}:$

$$
f(-2)=f(-1)=f(0)=f(1)=f(2)=f(3)=\frac{1}{6}
$$

Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =-2\cdot f(-2)+(-1)\cdot f(-1)+0\cdot f(0)+1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3) \\  & =-2(\frac{1}{6})+(-1)(\frac{1}{6})+0(\frac{1}{6})+1(\frac{1}{6})+2(\frac{1}{6})+3(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{6}-\frac{1}{6}+0+\frac{1}{6}+\frac{2}{6}+\frac{3}{6} \\  & =\frac{-2-1+0+1+2+3}{6} \\  & =\frac{3}{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-36c5b657-8ae8-52f1-9b50-9850b824e02a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-36c5b657-8ae8-52f1-9b50-9850b824e02a" :answer-field/id #uuid "36c5b657-8ae8-52f1-9b50-9850b824e02a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-e15daab7-6b24-5c89-8928-f0f9fcd1b856" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e15daab7-6b24-5c89-8928-f0f9fcd1b856"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e15daab7-6b24-5c89-8928-f0f9fcd1b856" :answer/id #uuid "e15daab7-6b24-5c89-8928-f0f9fcd1b856" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-522d89ff-41d6-50ec-8d1b-a4ada325fbc8" :question/id #uuid "522d89ff-41d6-50ec-8d1b-a4ada325fbc8" :question/math-academy-id "q-83981" :question/problem "A stack contains four cards, where each card is labeled $1$, $4$, $6$, or $9.$ If one card is randomly drawn, what is its expected value?" :question/worked-solution "The expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x).
$$

Let $X$ be the label on a randomly drawn card. Then the support is $S=\{1,4,6,9\},$ and the corresponding probabilities are all $\frac{1}{4}:$

$$
f(1)=f(4)=f(6)=f(9)=\frac{1}{4}
$$

Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =1\cdot f(1)+4\cdot f(4)+6\cdot f(6)+9\cdot f(9) \\  & =1(\frac{1}{4})+4(\frac{1}{4})+6(\frac{1}{4})+9(\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{4}{4}+\frac{6}{4}+\frac{9}{4} \\  & =\frac{1+4+6+9}{4} \\  & =\frac{20}{4} \\  & =5\,.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-850858f3-9f08-5b6d-b191-4d25dc883811"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x).
$$

Let $X$ be the value labeled on a randomly drawn card. Then the support is $S=\{4,10\}.$

In the stack there are $2$ cards labeled with four and $6$ cards labeled with ten (eight cards in total), so the probabilities are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(4) & =\frac{2}{8}=\frac{1}{4} \\ P(10) & =\frac{6}{8}=\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =4\cdot f(4)+10\cdot f(10) \\  & =4(\frac{1}{4})+10(\frac{3}{4}) \\  & =1+\frac{15}{2} \\  & =\frac{17}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e295c467-cba5-5269-8303-2482a80e3bd4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e295c467-cba5-5269-8303-2482a80e3bd4" :answer-field/id #uuid "e295c467-cba5-5269-8303-2482a80e3bd4" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-f48698d2-8399-5591-8858-d21e6e33a4a6" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f48698d2-8399-5591-8858-d21e6e33a4a6"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f48698d2-8399-5591-8858-d21e6e33a4a6" :answer/id #uuid "f48698d2-8399-5591-8858-d21e6e33a4a6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{17}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-700fffbb-cd63-5378-9077-32b4c2add6e6" :question/id #uuid "700fffbb-cd63-5378-9077-32b4c2add6e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-84067" :question/problem "Several children were asked how many siblings they have. | Number of siblings | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Number of Children | $1$ | $5$ | $3$ | $1$ |" :question/worked-solution "The expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x).
$$

We're given the frequencies of the number of siblings, so we can start by computing the corresponding probabilities. The total number of children is $1+5+3+1=10,$ so the corresponding probabilities are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=0)=f(0) & =\frac{1}{10} \\ P(X=1)=f(1) & =\frac{5}{10}=\frac{1}{2} \\ P(X=2)=f(2) & =\frac{3}{10} \\ P(X=3)=f(3) & =\frac{1}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

We organize these results in the table below.

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{10}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{3}{10}$ | $\frac{1}{10}$ |

Now, summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x).
$$

We're given the frequencies of the faulty items, so we can start by computing the corresponding probabilities. The total number of boxes is $13+6+4+2=25,$ so the corresponding probabilities are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=0)=f(0) & =\frac{13}{25} \\ P(X=1)=f(1) & =\frac{6}{25} \\ P(X=2)=f(2) & =\frac{4}{25} \\ P(X=3)=f(3) & =\frac{2}{25}\end{aligned}
$$

We organize these results in the table below.

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{13}{25}$ | $\frac{6}{25}$ | $\frac{4}{25}$ | $\frac{2}{25}$ |

Now, summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =0\cdot f(0)+1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3) \\  & =0(\frac{13}{25})+1(\frac{6}{25})+2(\frac{4}{25})+3(\frac{2}{25}) \\  & =\frac{6}{25}+\frac{8}{25}+\frac{6}{25} \\  & =\frac{6+8+6}{25} \\  & =\frac{20}{25} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}

- the ![](images/1d/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-coordinate equals the *sine* of the corresponding central angle.

Let's use the unit circle to list the special values of sine and cosine, starting with the first quadrant. First, we mark off the special angles in this quadrant.

In addition, we'll highlight the ![](images/1d/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-coordinate at each point.

But what about the other quadrants? 

The values in the remaining quadrants can be obtained from the coordinates in the first quadrant. Let's see how:

- To obtain the points in the *second* quadrant, let's first mark off the special angles in this quadrant. These angles have the same reference angles as the angles in the first quadrant:

- $180^\circ - 30^\circ = 150^\circ$

- $180^\circ - 45^\circ = 135^\circ$

- $180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ$

We mark these angles below and include the quadrantal angle $180^\circ.$

![](images/49/49105a62c4eecffeb32f6777ddf98022c5ca46079a33294e7eeafc9164444cba.png)

Now, we reflect the coordinates in the first quadrant in the $y$-axis. This changes the sign of the $x$-coordinate at each point and leaves the $y$-coordinate unchanged.

![](images/e4/e44980d06903b6570182b99787ca7dec8cceacab2f72dce04fc48b3d7c660059.png)

- To obtain the points in the third quadrant, we first find the special angles in this quadrant. Again, these angles have the same reference angles as the special angles in the first quadrant:

- $180^\circ + 30^\circ = 210^\circ$

- $180^\circ + 45^\circ = 225^\circ$

- $180^\circ + 60^\circ = 240^\circ$

Then, we take the points in the second quadrant and reflect them in the $x$-axis. This changes the sign of the $y$-coordinate at each point and leaves the $x$-coordinate unchanged.

![](images/bb/bbfcf14e39ee122cf1bd7048903ac7f205325c77d4b2899c53619495ffeb8d8c.png)

- Finally, to obtain the points in the fourth quadrant, we first compute the special angles in this quadrant:

- $360^\circ - 30^\circ = 330^\circ$

- $360^\circ - 45^\circ = 315^\circ$

- $360^\circ - 60^\circ = 300^\circ$

Then, we take the points in the first quadrant and reflect them in the $x$-axis. This changes the sign of the $y$-coordinate at each point and leaves the $x$-coordinate unchanged.

![](images/f5/f507964e8fe06cc54ceab447d570bb004b4e9a2b0b8fa3074762e28a41009a2a.png)

Therefore, our complete unit circle is as follows.

![](images/f5/f5006a5a3c363f83e6d4624fc72fefa140e29ef6ef23db16fbab5538b421a058.png)

$$
A=\{{n}^{2}∣n\in N\},\,B=\{\frac{2}{n}∣n\in N\}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $A=\{1,4,9,16,…\}$

II. $A\cap B=∅$

III. $A$ and $B$ are disjoint" :question/worked-solution "Two sets $A$ and $B$ are *disjoint* if they have no element in common, i.e., their intersection is empty:

$$
A\cap B=∅
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets.

- Statement I is true.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\{{n}^{2}∣n\in N\} \\  & =\{1,4,9,16,…\}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}B & =\{\frac{2}{n}∣n\in N\} \\  & =\{2,1,\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{2},…\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the intersection is 

$$
\begin{aligned}A\cap B & =\{1,4,9,16,…\}\text{ }\cap \{2,1,\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{2},…\} \\  & =\{1\}. \\  & \ne ∅.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the intersection is not empty, the two sets are not disjoint.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-13a24e13-db62-5670-988f-338080298b03"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-13a24e13-db62-5670-988f-338080298b03" :answer-field/id #uuid "13a24e13-db62-5670-988f-338080298b03" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-08ce1095-869e-5241-bc0f-d31e7ad9f8b3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5015133f-8d21-5500-88e1-9e6d7debce1d" "answer-08ce1095-869e-5241-bc0f-d31e7ad9f8b3" "answer-e27bcdd0-120e-5e1a-99dc-043eeeed575e" "answer-760c2ad4-3e54-558d-aea6-b33b0fda4022" "answer-383dc25d-8fd5-552d-8f79-44d5fd794297"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5015133f-8d21-5500-88e1-9e6d7debce1d" :answer/id #uuid "5015133f-8d21-5500-88e1-9e6d7debce1d" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-08ce1095-869e-5241-bc0f-d31e7ad9f8b3" :answer/id #uuid "08ce1095-869e-5241-bc0f-d31e7ad9f8b3" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e27bcdd0-120e-5e1a-99dc-043eeeed575e" :answer/id #uuid "e27bcdd0-120e-5e1a-99dc-043eeeed575e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-760c2ad4-3e54-558d-aea6-b33b0fda4022" :answer/id #uuid "760c2ad4-3e54-558d-aea6-b33b0fda4022" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-383dc25d-8fd5-552d-8f79-44d5fd794297" :answer/id #uuid "383dc25d-8fd5-552d-8f79-44d5fd794297" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-0803d7dd-fe65-5059-8e1e-9052cd416dca" :question/id #uuid "0803d7dd-fe65-5059-8e1e-9052cd416dca" :question/math-academy-id "q-174354" :question/problem "Which of the following pairs of sets are disjoint?

I. $\{x,y,z\}$ and $\{3,6,9\}$

II. $\{a,b,c,d,e\}$ and $\{a,e,i,o,u\}$

III. $\{1,3,6\}$ and $\{3,5,7\}$" :question/worked-solution "Two sets $A$ and $B$ are *disjoint* if they have no element in common, i.e., their intersection is empty:

$$
A\cap B=∅
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets.

- Pair I is disjoint. Indeed, the intersection of the sets is empty:

$$
\{x,y,z\}\cap \{3,6,9\}=∅\,\,✓
$$

- Pair II is *not* disjoint since the intersection of the sets is not empty:

$$
\{a,b,c,d,e\}\cap \{a,e,i,o,u\}=\{a,e\}\ne ∅\,\,\times
$$

- Pair III is *not* disjoint since the intersection of the sets is not empty:

$$
\{1,3,6\}\cap \{3,5,7\}=\{3\}\ne ∅\,\,\times
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d7d4f7d2-ef86-5eb2-85dd-e2f3c8149faa"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d7d4f7d2-ef86-5eb2-85dd-e2f3c8149faa" :answer-field/id #uuid "d7d4f7d2-ef86-5eb2-85dd-e2f3c8149faa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-d0d3c9d3-d1c2-58fc-b177-2a30b12c641b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e43a919e-dbae-5753-9e78-0bec425aa4d1" "answer-d0d3c9d3-d1c2-58fc-b177-2a30b12c641b" "answer-6c313729-f3be-5c18-ad10-2bc0c801ac14" "answer-ae87680f-698b-51a4-b00c-fd013d8a5ce6" "answer-05692866-4229-5d75-9f9d-452e956df231"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e43a919e-dbae-5753-9e78-0bec425aa4d1" :answer/id #uuid "e43a919e-dbae-5753-9e78-0bec425aa4d1" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d0d3c9d3-d1c2-58fc-b177-2a30b12c641b" :answer/id #uuid "d0d3c9d3-d1c2-58fc-b177-2a30b12c641b" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6c313729-f3be-5c18-ad10-2bc0c801ac14" :answer/id #uuid "6c313729-f3be-5c18-ad10-2bc0c801ac14" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ae87680f-698b-51a4-b00c-fd013d8a5ce6" :answer/id #uuid "ae87680f-698b-51a4-b00c-fd013d8a5ce6" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-05692866-4229-5d75-9f9d-452e956df231" :answer/id #uuid "05692866-4229-5d75-9f9d-452e956df231" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-4e68e4d1-4fbe-504a-90e3-9d792c948b3d" :question/id #uuid "4e68e4d1-4fbe-504a-90e3-9d792c948b3d" :question/math-academy-id "q-174361" :question/problem "Consider the following sets:

$$
A=\{n\in N∣n\le 5\},\,B=\{n\in N∣4n+6\ge 30\}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $B=\{6,7,8,…\}$

II. $A\cap B=∅$

III. $A$ and $B$ are disjoint" :question/worked-solution "Two sets $A$ and $B$ are *disjoint* if they have no element in common, i.e., their intersection is empty:

$$
A\cap B=∅
$$

First, notice that the elements of $B$ are positive integers that satisfy the inequality 

$$
\begin{aligned}4n+6 & \ge 30 \\ 4n & \ge 24 \\ n & \ge 6.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets.

- Statement I is true.

$$
\begin{aligned}B & =\{n\in N∣4n+6\ge 30\} \\  & =\{n\in N∣n\ge 6\} \\  & =\{6,7,8,…\}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\{n\in N∣n\le 5\} \\  & =\{1,2,3,4,5\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the intersection is 

$$
A\cap B=\{1,2,3,4,5\}\cap \{6,7,8,…\}=∅.
$$

- Statement III is true. Since the intersection is empty, the two sets are disjoint.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II and III."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1f9535db-621f-5f39-bbcf-0c1777901654"] :db/ensure #uuid "d4dcf09b-7fd5-51e9-80d9-32152841ce22" :question/math-academy-id "q-97989" :question/problem "Consider the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{bmatrix}$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=3.$ Given that $A$ has  eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=10$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ find the principal axes of the curve." :question/worked-solution "Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=3
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{bmatrix}-10\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields When the denominator contains two terms and includes radicals, we multiply both the numerator and the denominator by the *conjugate* of the denominator to eliminate the radical.

For example, consider the following expression:

$$
\dfrac{1}{1+\sqrt{x}}
$$

 

To find the conjugate of the denominator $1+\sqrt{x},$ all we have to do is flip the sign between the two terms. So, the conjugate of the denominator is 

$$
1\,{\color{blue}{-}}\,\sqrt{x}.
$$

Now, to rationalize the denominator, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by $1-\sqrt{x}$ and simplify:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{1+\sqrt{x}} & = \\ \frac{1}{1+\sqrt{x}}\cdot \frac{1-\sqrt{x}}{1-\sqrt{x}} & = \\ \frac{1-\sqrt{x}}{(1+\sqrt{x})(1-\sqrt{x})} & = \\ \frac{1-\sqrt{x}}{{1}^{2}-(\sqrt{x})^{2}} & = \\ \frac{1-\sqrt{x}}{1-x}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186213279 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [["question-047ba9d9-f028-5122-88f6-0f2794537abb" :question/id #uuid "047ba9d9-f028-5122-88f6-0f2794537abb"] ["question-047ba9d9-f028-5122-88f6-0f2794537abb" :question/math-academy-id "q-334280"] ["question-047ba9d9-f028-5122-88f6-0f2794537abb" :question/problem "$$

$$

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} \\ -2{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental matrix could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{3t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order."] ["question-047ba9d9-f028-5122-88f6-0f2794537abb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] "answer-field-5f77438e-6a65-5147-9492-745b947b2082"] [17592186059654 :knowledge-point/questions "question-9ede5978-9720-5b14-aefb-d172677e353f"] [17592186060882 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a general triangle where

- side $a$ is *opposite* angle $\angle A,$

- side $b$ is *opposite* angle $\angle B,$ and

- side $c$ is *opposite* angle $\angle C,$

as follows:

![](images/8f/8f3d3bf4824508ef152e8d8d567672d7d61fb36e0ffb533d97be7294e9198956.png)

The **law of cosines** states that

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2} & ={b}^{2}+{c}^{2}-2bc\operatorname{cos}⁡A \\ {b}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{c}^{2}-2ac\operatorname{cos}⁡B \\ {c}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{b}^{2}-2ab\operatorname{cos}⁡C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use this to calculate the length of one side when we know two sides and one angle.

If we look at the law of cosines we see that it's quite similar to the Pythagorean theorem:

$$
a^2+b^2=c^2
$$

But remember that the Pythagorean theorem can *only* be used for a *right-angled triangle*!

![](images/db/db9ed4aac9ca46ffc95d393d863cb09e9ba874caf0008410937f961fdf6c7ab6.png)

The law of cosines is more general and can be used on *any* triangle.

**Note:** To remember the law of cosines, it's helpful to notice that the equations always follow the same pattern:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{pmatrix}\,\text{side opposite}\, \\ \,\text{the angle}\,\end{pmatrix}}^{2}\,=\,{\begin{pmatrix}\,\text{adjacent}\, \\ \,\text{side}\,\end{pmatrix}}^{2}\,+\,{\begin{pmatrix}\,\text{adjacent}\, \\ \,\text{other side}\,\end{pmatrix}}^{2}\,-\,2\begin{pmatrix}\,\text{adjacent}\, \\ \,\text{side}\,\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\,\text{adjacent}\, \\ \,\text{other side}\,\end{pmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\text{angle}).\end{aligned}
$$

We'll show how this formula can be derived at the end of the lesson."] [17592186060884 :tutorial/content "Let's look at our general triangle again.

![](images/8f/8f3d3bf4824508ef152e8d8d567672d7d61fb36e0ffb533d97be7294e9198956.png)

When we know the lengths of three sides of a triangle, we rearrange the law of cosines to find an angle:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2} & ={b}^{2}+{c}^{2}-2bc\operatorname{cos}⁡A \\ 2bc\operatorname{cos}⁡A & ={b}^{2}+{c}^{2}-{a}^{2} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡A & =\frac{{b}^{2}+{c}^{2}-{a}^{2}}{2bc}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, for all the angles, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡A & =\frac{{b}^{2}+{c}^{2}-{a}^{2}}{2bc}, \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡B & =\frac{{a}^{2}+{c}^{2}-{b}^{2}}{2ac}, \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡C & =\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}-{c}^{2}}{2ab}.\end{aligned}
$$

It's helpful to notice that the equations always follow the same pattern:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\text{angle})=\frac{{\begin{pmatrix}\text{adjacent} \\ \text{side}\end{pmatrix}}^{2}+{\begin{pmatrix}\text{adjacent} \\ \text{other side}\end{pmatrix}}^{2}-{\begin{pmatrix}\text{side opposite} \\ \text{the angle}\end{pmatrix}}^{2}}{2\begin{pmatrix}\text{adjacent} \\ \text{side}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\text{adjacent} \\ \text{other side}\end{pmatrix}}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186060863 :tutorial/content "Let's now derive the law of cosines in the following form:

$$
a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A
$$

Consider $\triangle ABC$ with sides of lengths $a,b,$ and $c,$ as shown below. 

![](images/7c/7cc2a0cbb6a02af829e070fc54cfdbe616683f86527b119a530053a34048e699.png)

Let's now add the height $\overline{CH}$ and assume it has length $h,$ as shown.

![](images/d4/d4e80b2b54283ea353b687d959e9d8fc6c9303e85081c0a46b48703ee3dae7d5.png)

The remainder of this proof consists of two steps:

- **Step 1**: Write down expressions for $\cos A$ and $\sin A.$

- **Step 2**: Apply the Pythagorean theorem to $\triangle BHC,$ and simplify.

Using elementary trigonometry, we have

$$
\cos A = \dfrac{AH}{b}, \qquad \sin A = \dfrac{h}{b},
$$

which can be written as

$$
AH =  b\cos A, \qquad h = b\sin A.
$$

Applying the Pythagorean theorem to $\triangle BHC$ and using our expression for $h,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2} & =(BH)^{2}+{h}^{2} \\ {a}^{2} & =(BH)^{2}+{b}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the length of the side $\overline{AB}.$ Since $\overline{AB}$ consists of two segments, $\overline{AH}$ and $\overline{BH},$ we have

$$
c = AH + BH\quad \Longrightarrow\quad BH = c - AH,
$$

and using our expression for $AH,$ we have

$$
BH = c - b\cos A.
$$

Substituting this into our expression for $a^2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2} & =(BH)^{2}+{b}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡A \\  & =(c-b\operatorname{cos}⁡A)^{2}+{b}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡A \\  & ={c}^{2}-2bc\operatorname{cos}⁡A+{b}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡A+{b}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡A \\  & ={b}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡A+{b}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡A+{c}^{2}-2bc\operatorname{cos}⁡A \\  & ={b}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡A+{sin}^{2}⁡A)+{c}^{2}-2bc\operatorname{cos}⁡A.\end{aligned}
$$

It can be shown that $\cos^2A + \sin^2 A = 1$ for any angle $A$ (this is the Pythagorean theorem in trigonometric form). Therefore, we have

$$
a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A
$$

as required.

We can use a similar argument to prove the following results:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}^{2} &={a}^{2}+{c}^{2}-2ac\operatorname{cos}⁡B \\ {c}^{2} &={a}^{2}+{b}^{2}-2ab\operatorname{cos}⁡C\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186059897 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0] ["question-19a2dc0a-21a4-5b89-85c8-47422a295e17" :question/id #uuid "19a2dc0a-21a4-5b89-85c8-47422a295e17"] ["question-19a2dc0a-21a4-5b89-85c8-47422a295e17" :question/math-academy-id "q-974"] ["question-19a2dc0a-21a4-5b89-85c8-47422a295e17" :question/problem "Given that $\frac{5}{2}\cdot {3}^{x}=5,$ find the value of $x$ rounded to $3$ decimal places."] ["question-19a2dc0a-21a4-5b89-85c8-47422a295e17" :question/worked-solution "First, we rearrange our equation into a form that is more convenient for logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2}\cdot {3}^{x} & =5 \\ {3}^{x} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we take ${log}_{3}$ of both sides of the equation and solve for $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{x} & =2 \\ {log}_{3}⁡({3}^{x}) & ={log}_{3}⁡(2) \\ x & ={log}_{3}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we rewrite the right-hand side using the change of base formula:

$$
x=\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}
$$

Evaluating the above on a calculator gives

$$
x≈0.631
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."] ["question-19a2dc0a-21a4-5b89-85c8-47422a295e17" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-f58ba2f4-b668-5a8c-92f5-c9264d481c97" :answer-field/id $$
\begin{aligned}{11}^{2x-3} & =\sqrt[3]{{7}^{2}} \\ {log}_{11}⁡({11}^{2x-3}) & ={log}_{11}⁡(\sqrt[3]{{7}^{2}}) \\ 2x-3 & ={log}_{11}⁡({7}^{2/3})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the power rule to the right-hand side:

$$
2x-3=\frac{2}{3}{log}_{11}⁡(7)
$$

Next, we rewrite the right-hand side using the change of base formula and then solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-3 & =\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(7)}{3\operatorname{log}⁡(11)} \\ 2x & =\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(7)}{3\operatorname{log}⁡(11)}+3 \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(7)}{3\operatorname{log}⁡(11)}+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the above on a calculator gives

$$
x≈1.771
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."] ["question-fa39cf5e-b1cf-510a-a444-4f30da1c63f4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-335d885a-d13c-55bb-8478-3d052924914c" :answer-field/id $$
\begin{aligned}{7}^{5x}+8 & =34 \\ {7}^{5x} & =26\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{7}^{5x} & =26 \\ {log}_{7}⁡({7}^{5x}) & ={log}_{7}⁡(26) \\ 5x & ={log}_{7}⁡(26) \\ x & =\frac{1}{5}{log}_{7}⁡(26)\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the above on a calculator gives

$$
x≈0.335
$$

$$
(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),
$$

where $p$ is constant.

$$
(y-2)^{2}=4(6)(x-0).
$$

It is now clear that our equation is of the standard type with $p=6.$

["question-42a89ddb-b42b-5afd-9218-01f794cbc72e" :question/math-academy-id "q-67501"] ["question-42a89ddb-b42b-5afd-9218-01f794cbc72e" :question/problem "Which of the three sequences below are geometric sequences?

I. $\frac{1}{4},\,\frac{1}{2},\,2,\,…$

II. ${a}_{n+1}=\frac{3}{2}{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=-1,\,n\ge 1$

III. $1,\,0.2,\,0.03,\,…$"] ["question-42a89ddb-b42b-5afd-9218-01f794cbc72e" :question/worked-solution "A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is not a geometric sequence because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{(\frac{1}{4})} & =2 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{2}{(\frac{1}{2})} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is a geometric sequence. The recursive rule ${a}_{n+1}=\frac{3}{2}{a}_{n}$ tells us that each term is $\frac{3}{2}$ times the previous term, so the common ratio is $r=\frac{3}{2}.$

- Sequence III is not a geometric sequence because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{0.2}{1} & =0.2 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{0.03}{0.2} & =0.15\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only sequence II is a geometric sequence."] ["question-42a89ddb-b42b-5afd-9218-01f794cbc72e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] :question/problem "What is the $4$th term of the geometric sequence given below?

$$
{a}_{n+1}=-6{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=\frac{1}{36},\,n\ge 1
$$"] ["question-857b63a1-09cd-5ba9-9404-4c37877c9864" :question/worked-solution "We use the recursive formula to compute the terms of the sequence up to the $4$th term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =\frac{1}{36} \\ {a}_{2} & =-6{a}_{1}=-6(\frac{1}{36})=-\frac{1}{6} \\ {a}_{3} & =-6{a}_{2}=-6(-\frac{1}{6})=1 \\ {a}_{4} & =-6{a}_{3}=-6(1)=-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${a}_{4}=-6.$"] ["question-857b63a1-09cd-5ba9-9404-4c37877c9864" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-e8f8080f-0b51-545f-9d71-93e2c857b6d4" :answer-field/id ["question-244be0b4-aca1-5c1c-abe2-94099e0fbbe5" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{z+y-{x}^{2}}?$

I. The partial derivative with respect to $x$ is defined at $(0,0,1)$

II. ${f}_{y}(1,2,0)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{z}(1,1,0)$ is defined"] ["question-244be0b4-aca1-5c1c-abe2-94099e0fbbe5" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{x}{\sqrt{z+y-{x}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z+y-{x}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z+y-{x}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(0,0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,0,1)=\sqrt{1+0-{0}^{2}}=1,
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(0,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,0,1) & =-\frac{0}{\sqrt{1+0-{0}^{2}}}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,2,0)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,2,0)=\sqrt{0+2-{1}^{2}}=1,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(1,2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,2,0) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{0+2-{1}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(1,1,0)$ into ${f}_{z}$, we get

$$
{f}_{z}(1,1,0)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{0+1-{1}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I and II only'."] ["question-244be0b4-aca1-5c1c-abe2-94099e0fbbe5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] equation ${x}^{2}{e}^{3x}-4x{e}^{3x}-12{e}^{3x}=0?$"] ["question-12b67edd-e409-5ea0-9859-9fa94b363ebb" :question/worked-solution "First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{e}^{3x}-4x{e}^{3x}-12{e}^{3x} & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}-4x-12){e}^{3x} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can now apply the zero product property, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0.$ This gives us two equations,

$$
{x}^{2}-4x-12=0\,\text{and}\,{e}^{3x}=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- The equation ${x}^{2}-4x-12=0$ can be factored as

$$
(x+2)(x-6)=0,
$$

which leads to the solutions $x=-2,6.$

- The equation ${e}^{3x}=0$ has no solutions because ${e}^{3x}$ is positive for every real number $x.$

Therefore, the original equation has the solutions $x=-2,6,$ and their product is $(-2)\cdot 6=-12.$"] ["question-12b67edd-e409-5ea0-9859-9fa94b363ebb" :question/difficulty :question/worked-solution "First, we factor the equation:

  

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}\cdot {5}^{x} & =11x\cdot {5}^{x}+4\cdot {5}^{x} \\ 3{x}^{2}\cdot {5}^{x}-11x\cdot {5}^{x}-4\cdot {5}^{x} & =0 \\ (3{x}^{2}-11x-4)\cdot {5}^{x} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can now apply the zero product property, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0.$ This gives us two equations,

$$
3{x}^{2}-11x-4=0\,\text{and}\,{5}^{x}=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- The equation $3{x}^{2}-11x-4=0$ can be factored as

$$
(3x+1)(x-4)=0,
$$

which leads to the solutions $x=-\frac{1}{3},4.$

- The equation ${5}^{x}=0$ has no solutions because ${5}^{x}$ is positive for every real number $x.$

Therefore, the original equation has the solutions $x=-\frac{1}{3},4,$ and their product is $(-\frac{1}{3})\cdot 4=-\frac{4}{3}.$"] ["question-e2c0ab81-ce73-5f44-b936-e8bb7ee9594f" $$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}{e}^{x} & =36{e}^{x} \\ 9{x}^{2}{e}^{x}-36{e}^{x} & =0 \\ (9{x}^{2}-36){e}^{x} & =0\end{aligned}

$$

$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

$$
(3x+6)(3x-6)=0,
$$

which leads to the solutions $x=-2,2.$

- The equation ${e}^{x}=0$ has no solutions because ${e}^{x}$ is positive for every real number $x.$

- Let's first consider the angle ${180}^{∘}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle ${180}^{∘}$ corresponds to the point $(-1,0).$  Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}⁡({180}^{∘})=-1.$ Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡({180}^{∘})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡({180}^{∘})}=\frac{1}{-1}=-1.
$$

- Now, let's consider the angle ${90}^{∘}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle ${90}^{∘}$ corresponds to the point $(0,1).$  Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}⁡({90}^{∘})=1.$ Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡({90}^{∘})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡({90}^{∘})}=\frac{1}{1}=1.
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡({180}^{∘})+\operatorname{csc}⁡({90}^{∘})=-1+1=0.
$$"] ["question-621a7d94-aa15-5da2-a86e-6e37bead83f1" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-99de1166-6614-59dc-ba88-9b3adbcbf5e8" :answer-field/id #uuid "answer-field-2ba2b05c-984d-5188-ba82-e7eff754bb83"] [17592186059842 :knowledge-point/questions "question-5dc0c374-75b0-5038-a236-6349d3712634"] [17592186060905 :tutorial/content "A **quadrantal angle** is an angle whose terminal side lies on the $x$ or $y$-axis. 
The unit circle below illustrates the quadrantal angles that lie on the range $[0^\circ, 360^\circ).$

![](images/79/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

We can identify four points on the unit circle above,

$$
(1,0), \quad (0,1), \quad (-1,0), \quad (0,-1),
$$

that correspond to the angles

$$
0^\circ, \quad 90^\circ,\quad 180^\circ, \quad 270^\circ,
$$

in degrees, or

$$
0, \quad \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \quad \pi, \quad \dfrac{3\pi}{2},
$$

in radians.

We can use these points to find cosine and sine of quadrantal angles. First, recall that a point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta$ using the following formulas:

$$
x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta
$$

For example, if we are asked to find the value of $\cos(\pi),$ then we just look at the $\color{blue}x$-coordinate of the corresponding point. The point is $({\color{blue}{-1}},0),$ and therefore, we get

$$
\cos(\pi)={\color{blue}{-1}}.
$$"] [17592186059944 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-272bf8c6-2369-5e98-9adb-ebe6db7bece2" :question/id #uuid "272bf8c6-2369-5e98-9adb-ebe6db7bece2"] ["question-272bf8c6-2369-5e98-9adb-ebe6db7bece2" :question/math-academy-id "q-257192"] ["question-272bf8c6-2369-5e98-9adb-ebe6db7bece2" :question/problem "Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-2,2]\times [0,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where

{{field-1}}

</tbody></table>"] ["question-272bf8c6-2369-5e98-9adb-ebe6db7bece2" :question/worked-solution "The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}y-x\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}y-x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y-x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{y}^{2}+6 & 8xy-1 \\ 8xy-1 & 4{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}4{y}^{2}+6 & 8xy-1 \\ 8xy-1 & 4{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}y-x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}4{y}^{2}+6 & 8xy-1 \\ 8xy-1 & 4{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}y-x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}4(0)^{2}+6 & 8(-1)(0)-1 \\ 8(-1)(0)-1 & 4(-1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}4(-1)(0)^{2}+6(-1)-0-2 \\ 4(-1)^{2}(0)-(-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}6 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{6\cdot 4-(-1)\cdot (-1)}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{23}\begin{bmatrix}-31 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}0.348 \\ 0.087\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-272bf8c6-2369-5e98-9adb-ebe6db7bece2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-9ae66afd-66cd-529a-9898-9254316b1674" :answer-field/id #uuid "9ae66afd-66cd-529a-9898-9254316b1674"] ["answer-fae98102-ed44-578d-91b3-534204bfeae8" :answer/id #uuid "fae98102-ed44-578d-91b3-534204bfeae8"] ["answer-fae98102-ed44-578d-91b3-534204bfeae8" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-fae98102-ed44-578d-91b3-534204bfeae8" :answer/value "0.087"] ["answer-field-9ae66afd-66cd-529a-9898-9254316b1674" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-9ae66afd-66cd-529a-9898-9254316b1674" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-9ae66afd-66cd-529a-9898-9254316b1674" :answer-field/correct "answer-fae98102-ed44-578d-91b3-534204bfeae8"] ["answer-field-9ae66afd-66cd-529a-9898-9254316b1674" :answer-field/choices "answer-fae98102-ed44-578d-91b3-534204bfeae8"] ["question-272bf8c6-2369-5e98-9adb-ebe6db7bece2" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-9ae66afd-66cd-529a-9898-9254316b1674"] [17592186204024 :knowledge-point/questions "question-272bf8c6-2369-5e98-9adb-ebe6db7bece2"] ["question-cd16fbf2-f5ff-5242-b610-fb61c79ec2b3" :question/id #uuid "cd16fbf2-f5ff-5242-b610-fb61c79ec2b3"] ["question-cd16fbf2-f5ff-5242-b610-fb61c79ec2b3" :question/math-academy-id "q-257191"] ["question-cd16fbf2-f5ff-5242-b610-fb61c79ec2b3" :question/problem "Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-2,0]\times [-2,0]⊆{R}^{2},$ where

$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}+{y}^{4}-4{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}+10) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{4}+{y}^{4}-4{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}+10)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{x}^{3}-8x \\ 4{y}^{3}-8y\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}

and the Hessian is

$$

$$

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}12{x}^{2}-8 & 0 \\ 0 & 12{y}^{2}-8\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}4{x}^{3}-8x \\ 4{y}^{3}-8y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-6y+13) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-6y+13)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}-6x \\ 3{y}^{2}-6\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-6x) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(3{y}^{2}-6) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-6x) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{y}^{2}-6)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6x-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}6x-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}-6x \\ 3{y}^{2}-6\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}6x-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}-6x \\ 3{y}^{2}-6\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2.25 \\ 1.5\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}6(2.25)-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6(1.5)\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}3(2.25)^{2}-6(2.25) \\ 3(1.5)^{2}-6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2.25 \\ 1.5\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}7.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 9\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}1.6875 \\ 0.75\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2.25 \\ 1.5\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{7.5\cdot 9-0\cdot 0}\begin{bmatrix}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 7.5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1.6875 \\ 0.75\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2.25 \\ 1.5\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{67.5}\begin{bmatrix}15.1875 \\ 5.625\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}2.025 \\ 1.417\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-11575fd3-3b68-5f5f-9c8d-ffa66ae7367b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-d4e92ca9-095d-5013-a0f3-2a43f9ecb853" :answer-field/id #uuid "d4e92ca9-095d-5013-a0f3-2a43f9ecb853"] ["answer-ccb984f5-1d1e-5d3d-89ea-171fda9ca2b4" :answer/id #uuid "ccb984f5-1d1e-5d3d-89ea-171fda9ca2b4"] ["answer-ccb984f5-1d1e-5d3d-89ea-171fda9ca2b4" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-ccb984f5-1d1e-5d3d-89ea-171fda9ca2b4" :answer/value "2.025"] ["answer-field-d4e92ca9-095d-5013-a0f3-2a43f9ecb853" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-d4e92ca9-095d-5013-a0f3-2a43f9ecb853" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-d4e92ca9-095d-5013-a0f3-2a43f9ecb853" :answer-field/correct "answer-ccb984f5-1d1e-5d3d-89ea-171fda9ca2b4"] ["answer-field-d4e92ca9-095d-5013-a0f3-2a43f9ecb853" :answer-field/choices "answer-ccb984f5-1d1e-5d3d-89ea-171fda9ca2b4"] ["question-11575fd3-3b68-5f5f-9c8d-ffa66ae7367b" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-d4e92ca9-095d-5013-a0f3-2a43f9ecb853"] [17592186204025 :knowledge-point/questions "question-11575fd3-3b68-5f5f-9c8d-ffa66ae7367b"] ["question-e391a05d-f936-58b5-934a-ad5b4d40ee91" :question/id #uuid "e391a05d-f936-58b5-934a-ad5b4d40ee91"] ["question-e391a05d-f936-58b5-934a-ad5b4d40ee91" :question/math-academy-id "q-257213"] ["question-e391a05d-f936-58b5-934a-ad5b4d40ee91" :question/problem "Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,1]\times [-1,0]⊆{R}^{2},$ where

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be rewritten as

$$
{H}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-∇f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(5x{y}^{2}-2xy-{x}^{2}+3y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(5x{y}^{2}-2xy-{x}^{2}+3y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5{y}^{2}-2y-2x \\ 10xy-2x+3\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(5{y}^{2}-2y-2x) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(10xy-2x+3) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(5{y}^{2}-2y-2x) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(10xy-2x+3)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 10y-2 \\ 10y-2 & 10x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 10y-2 \\ 10y-2 & 10x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{\begin{bmatrix}5{y}^{2}-2y-2x \\ 10xy-2x+3\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 10y-2 \\ 10y-2 & 10x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{\begin{bmatrix}5{y}^{2}-2y-2x \\ 10xy-2x+3\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-2 & 10(-1)-2 \\ 10(-1)-2 & 10(1)\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-\begin{bmatrix}5(-1)^{2}-2(-1)-2(1) \\ 10(1)(-1)-2(1)+3\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-2 & -12 \\ -12 & 10\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get $({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}-29/82 \\ 39/82\end{bmatrix}.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{29}{82} \\ \frac{39}{82}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{29}{82} \\ \frac{39}{82}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}0.646 \\ -0.524\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e391a05d-f936-58b5-934a-ad5b4d40ee91" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-a1efd346-8fdf-5f03-b6fe-b0884388016a" :answer-field/id #uuid </tbody></table>"] ["question-ce47ce1b-5e64-5fb8-88b0-27f2349480f8" :question/worked-solution "The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be rewritten as

$$
{H}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-∇f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(6x{y}^{2}-3{x}^{2}-6xy+2x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(6x{y}^{2}-3{x}^{2}-6xy+2x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2 \\ 12xy-6x\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(12xy-6x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(12xy-6x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 12y-6 \\ 12y-6 & 12x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 12y-6 \\ 12y-6 & 12x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{\begin{bmatrix}6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2 \\ 12xy-6x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 12y-6 \\ 12y-6 & 12x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{\begin{bmatrix}6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2 \\ 12xy-6x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-6 & 12(1)-6 \\ 12(1)-6 & 12(0)\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-\begin{bmatrix}6(1)^{2}-6(0)-6(1)+2 \\ 12(0)(1)-6(0)\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-6 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get $({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1/3\end{bmatrix}.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0.667\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ce47ce1b-5e64-5fb8-88b0-27f2349480f8" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-4723ac7c-15e6-5105-8cff-0c025fd5d952" :answer-field/id #uuid {H}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-∇f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}-xy+x-y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}-xy+x-y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-y+1 \\ -4xy-x-1\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-y+1) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(-4xy-x-1) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-y+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(-4xy-x-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6x & -4y-1 \\ -4y-1 & -4x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}6x & -4y-1 \\ -4y-1 & -4x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-y+1 \\ -4xy-x-1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}6x & -4y-1 \\ -4y-1 & -4x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-y+1 \\ -4xy-x-1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}6(-1) & -4(1)-1 \\ -4(1)-1 & -4(-1)\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-\begin{bmatrix}3(-1)^{2}-2(1)^{2}-1+1 \\ -4(-1)(1)-(-1)-1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-6 & -5 \\ -5 & 4\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get $({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}24/49 \\ -19/49\end{bmatrix}.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+\begin{bmatrix}\frac{24}{49} \\ -\frac{19}{49}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\frac{24}{49} \\ -\frac{19}{49}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}-0.510 \\ 0.612\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-4033d90f-6820-5b6e-97e2-e268a68a992f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-1efb643c-734b-58b8-990d-a15c076650e6" :answer-field/id #uuid the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[1,2]\times [0,1]⊆{R}^{2},$ where

$$
f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y-4x-2y-2{y}^{2}.
$$

Fill in the blanks in the matrix equation below that defines the first iteration of the Newton-Raphson process starting at the point $[2,\,1]^{T}.$

<td align="center" rowspan="2">$[$</td>

</td>
<td align="center" rowspan="2">$]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})\,=[$</td>

<tr>

<td align="center" height="25" width="25">
$-4$
</td>
<td align="center" height="25" width="25">
$-2$
</td>

</tbody></table>"] ["question-5acc736b-d0d8-5439-9126-2975fad286b2" :question/worked-solution "The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be rewritten as

$$
{H}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-∇f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}y-4x-2y-2{y}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}y-4x-2y-2{y}^{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4xy-4 \\ 2{x}^{2}-2-4y\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy-4) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-2-4y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy-4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-2-4y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4y & 4x \\ 4x & -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}4y & 4x \\ 4x & -4\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{\begin{bmatrix}4xy-4 \\ 2{x}^{2}-2-4y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}4y & 4x \\ 4x & -4\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{\begin{bmatrix}4xy-4 \\ 2{x}^{2}-2-4y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}4(1) & 4(2) \\ 4(2) & -4\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-\begin{bmatrix}4(2)(1)-4 \\ 2(2)^{2}-2-4(1)\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}4 & 8 \\ 8 & -4\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-5acc736b-d0d8-5439-9126-2975fad286b2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-a16d0722-b98a-5c1d-95f0-119e1fc538e4" :answer-field/id #uuid "Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-x+2y &=-1 \\ 4x-8y &=4 \\ -4x+8y &=-4.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system."] ["question-35e39332-390d-57d5-8a71-b2e823ef2c1d" :question/worked-solution "The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & -8 & 4 \\ -4 & 8 & -4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using the standard Gauss-Jordan method, we can reduce this matrix to reduced row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & -8 & 4 \\ -4 & 8 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & -8 & 4 \\ -4 & 8 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 8 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now  

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and we have one free variable, $y.$ That means we need to find $x$  in terms of $y.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=2y+1 \\ y &=y,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $y$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2y+1 \\ y\end{bmatrix},\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-35e39332-390d-57d5-8a71-b2e823ef2c1d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-5be30950-b64e-577a-ae02-66dc69074ea6" :answer-field/id #uuid \left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y+z &=4 \\ y-3z &=-1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system."] ["question-0d9a8a04-d6f4-5dae-8ede-86bd3b61ce86" :question/worked-solution "The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using the standard Gauss-Jordan method, we can reduce this matrix to reduced row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -5 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now  

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-5z &=2 \\ y-3z &=-1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are $x$ and $y,$ and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=5z+2 \\ y &=3z-1 \\ z &=z,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $z$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5z+2 \\ 3z-1 \\ z\end{bmatrix},\,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-0d9a8a04-d6f4-5dae-8ede-86bd3b61ce86" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-38a28058-8837-5c47-bd4f-999f7f79529b" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Consider the following system of equations.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-x+y &=-1 \\ 2x+3y &=3 \\ -x-4y &=-3.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. The system is inconsistent

II. The system has a unique solution

III. The system is consistent dependent"] ["question-2f4a72f8-3bd3-5788-9d12-62ca6f611891" :question/worked-solution "To classify the system, we first need to find its solution. The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 & 3 \\ -1 & -4 & -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using the method of Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 & 3 \\ -1 & -4 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 \\ -1 & -4 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & -5 & -2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The final row corresponds to the equation $0x+0y=-1,$ and this has no solution. Therefore, our system has no solution, and we conclude that the system is inconsistent.

As a result, only statement I is true."] ["question-2f4a72f8-3bd3-5788-9d12-62ca6f611891" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-eda18abf-1e9e-51ea-a1af-55bc7948bea6"
