:question/problem "Consider the polar curve $r={cos}^{2}⁡\theta$ for $\theta \in [0,\pi ).$ Given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ),
$$

and ${x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0$

II. ${lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=0$

III. The curve has a horizontal tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$

*Hint: It is not necessary to use L'Hopital's rule to evaluate the limit in part II.*"] ["question-fcf32a74-971a-505b-b459-ef18eedf0a90" :question/worked-solution "When a polar curve is differentiable at a point ${\theta }_{0}$, there is a horizontal tangent at ${\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}=0
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative ${y}^{′}(x)$ takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a horizontal tangent at this point if

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=0.
$$

In this case, we're told that ${x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${y}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})({cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Computing the limit as $\theta \to \frac{\pi }{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta ){cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}(\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta ){cos}^{\cancel{2}}⁡(\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}) \\  & =\frac{0-2\cdot 1}{-3\cdot 1\cdot 0} \\  & =\frac{-2}{0} \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the limit in part II does *not* equal to $0,$ there curve does *not* have a horizontal tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}.$ In fact, it is a vertical tangent.

![](images/f4/f4609e6433a861ef255cbeeac60c8a316e5c14a89df45030e26e526e3a1253a4.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""] ["question-fcf32a74-971a-505b-b459-ef18eedf0a90" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-e16e2010-e951-50c2-8dc9-1ddcbae83f31" :question/problem "Consider the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{3}⁡\theta$ for $\theta \in [0,\pi ).$ Given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )={cos}^{3}⁡\theta \,(5{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -4),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta (5{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -3),
$$

and ${x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0$

II. ${lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=0$

III. The curve has a horizontal tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$

*Hint: It is not necessary to use L'Hopital's rule to evaluate the limit in part II.*"] ["question-3f8bf9ef-a3d1-5fa9-97cc-d10fddcf1cd1" :question/worked-solution "When a polar curve is differentiable at a point ${\theta }_{0}$, there is a horizontal tangent at ${\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}=0
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative ${y}^{′}(x)$ takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a horizontal tangent at this point if

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=0.
$$

In this case, we're told that ${x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${y}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}){cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})(5{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-3) \\  & =1\cdot 0\cdot (5\cdot 0-3) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Computing the limit as $\theta \to \frac{\pi }{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,(5{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -3)}{{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \,(5{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -4)}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\cancel{cos}}^{2}\theta \,(5{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -3)}{{cos}^{\cancel{3}}⁡\theta \,(5{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -4)}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to \pi /2}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,(5{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -3)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,(5{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -4)}) \\  & =\frac{1\cdot (5\cdot 0-3)}{0\cdot (5\cdot 0-4)} \\  & =\frac{-3}{0} \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the limit in part II does *not* equal to $0,$ there curve does *not* have a horizontal tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}.$ In fact, it is a vertical tangent.

![](images/d7/d7881ba860bcc32301a162eb200ea9075b06b63c780be74c14aedbcb1654eaaa.png)

["question-1355c292-a399-578d-8bac-2939b3befda0" :question/math-academy-id "q-145039"] ["question-1355c292-a399-578d-8bac-2939b3befda0" :question/problem "Consider the polar curve $r={cos}^{2}⁡\theta$ for $\theta \in [0,\pi ).$ Given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ),
$$

and ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0$

II. ${lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\infty$

III. The curve has a vertical tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$"] ["question-1355c292-a399-578d-8bac-2939b3befda0" :question/worked-solution "For a given polar curve, there is a vertical tangent at $\theta ={\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a vertical tangent at this point if

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty \,\text{and}\,{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty .
$$

In this case, we're told that ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${x}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}){cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-3\cdot 1\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Computing the limit as $\theta \to {(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{+},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta }) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{\cancel{cos}\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{\cancel{2}}⁡\theta }) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}) \\  & =\frac{0-2\cdot 1}{-3\cdot 1\cdot {0}^{-}} \\  & =\frac{-2}{{0}^{+}} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Using the calculations from part II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}) \\  & =\frac{0-2\cdot 1}{-3\cdot 1\cdot {0}^{+}} \\  & =\frac{-2}{{0}^{-}} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Since the limits of our derivative are both infinite, there is a vertical tangent to the curve at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}.$

![](images/50/50637a502a56fc242ba5d8e2fda59ddc899295d4b14f7ae692869536b95ef661.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""] ["question-1355c292-a399-578d-8bac-2939b3befda0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-54e659be-f31e-5f00-888e-77687d0dffe4" :question/worked-solution "The domain of $y=\sqrt[4]{x}$ is

$$
x\ge 0.
$$

To find the domain of $q(x)=2\sqrt[4]{x+3}-2,$ we replace $x$ with $x+3$ in the above inequality. This gives

$$
x+3\ge 0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+3 & \ge 0 \\ x & \ge -3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain of $y=q(x)$ is $x\in [-3,\infty ).$

We can also see that this is true from the graph of the function. The graph of $y=q(x)$ is shown below.

["question-7823b972-423e-5466-806b-703ca14c80f8" :question/worked-solution "The domain of $y=\sqrt[6]{x}$ is

$$
x\ge 0.
$$

To find the domain of $s(x)=\sqrt[6]{2x-4}+1,$ we replace $x$ with $2x-4$ in the above inequality. This gives

$$
2x-4\ge 0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-4 & \ge 0 \\ 2x & \ge 4 \\ x & \ge 2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain of $y=s(x)$ is $x\in [2,\infty ).$ 

We can also see that this is true from the graph of the function. The graph of $y=s(x)$ is shown below.

$A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -5 & 6\end{bmatrix}$ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $L=$"] ["question-903883c2-c07e-50f2-a202-1c38e08cadfc" :question/worked-solution "To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -5 & 6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+5{R}_{1}\,⟺\,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 5 & 1\end{bmatrix}}}\cdot A \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

["question-9cdf7c4f-4409-57f0-b1eb-dca5de834f65" :question/problem "A fair spinner has six sides labeled with the numbers $-2,$ $-1,$ $0,$ $1,$ $2,$ and $3.$ If the spinner is spun, what is the expected value of the outcome?

$\text{E}[X]=$
{{field-1}}"] ["question-9cdf7c4f-4409-57f0-b1eb-dca5de834f65" :question/worked-solution "The expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x).
$$

Let $X$ be the outcome of the spinner. Then the support is $S=\{-2,-1,0,1,2,3\},$ and the corresponding probabilities are all $\frac{1}{6}:$

$$
f(-2)=f(-1)=f(0)=f(1)=f(2)=f(3)=\frac{1}{6}
$$

Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =-2\cdot f(-2)+(-1)\cdot f(-1)+0\cdot f(0)+1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3) \\  & =-2(\frac{1}{6})+(-1)(\frac{1}{6})+0(\frac{1}{6})+1(\frac{1}{6})+2(\frac{1}{6})+3(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{6}-\frac{1}{6}+0+\frac{1}{6}+\frac{2}{6}+\frac{3}{6} \\  & =\frac{-2-1+0+1+2+3}{6} \\  & =\frac{3}{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}"] ["question-ceddea1b-a5cb-5c22-91ab-6571fb7ef388" :question/worked-solution "The expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x).
$$

Let $X$ be the value labeled on a randomly drawn card. Then the support is $S=\{4,10\}.$

In the stack there are $2$ cards labeled with four and $6$ cards labeled with ten (eight cards in total), so the probabilities are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(4) & =\frac{2}{8}=\frac{1}{4} \\ P(10) & =\frac{6}{8}=\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =4\cdot f(4)+10\cdot f(10) \\  & =4(\frac{1}{4})+10(\frac{3}{4}) \\  & =1+\frac{15}{2} \\  & =\frac{17}{2}.\end{aligned}

| $f(w)$ | $\frac{1}{38}$ | $\frac{37}{38}$ |

$$

$$
100\cdot \text{E}[W]=100\cdot (0.92)=92.
$$

Now, subtracting the $100$ dollars paid to play, we get that the expected profit (in dollars) is

$$

- To obtain the points in the *second* quadrant, let's first mark off the special angles in this quadrant. These angles have the same reference angles as the angles in the first quadrant:

- $180^\circ - 30^\circ = 150^\circ$

- $180^\circ - 45^\circ = 135^\circ$

- $180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ$

We mark these angles below and include the quadrantal angle $180^\circ.$

![](images/49/49105a62c4eecffeb32f6777ddf98022c5ca46079a33294e7eeafc9164444cba.png)

- To obtain the points in the third quadrant, we first find the special angles in this quadrant. Again, these angles have the same reference angles as the special angles in the first quadrant:

- $180^\circ + 30^\circ = 210^\circ$

- $180^\circ + 45^\circ = 225^\circ$

- $180^\circ + 60^\circ = 240^\circ$

Then, we take the points in the second quadrant and reflect them in the $x$-axis. This changes the sign of the $y$-coordinate at each point and leaves the $x$-coordinate unchanged.

- $360^\circ - 30^\circ = 330^\circ$

- $360^\circ - 45^\circ = 315^\circ$

Then, we take the points in the first quadrant and reflect them in the $x$-axis. This changes the sign of the $y$-coordinate at each point and leaves the $x$-coordinate unchanged.

$$
A=\{{n}^{2}∣n\in N\},\,B=\{\frac{2}{n}∣n\in N\}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $A=\{1,4,9,16,…\}$

II. $A\cap B=∅$

III. $A$ and $B$ are disjoint"] ["question-37c3bc23-bd02-5d58-b8ef-2de055e363b9" :question/worked-solution "Two sets $A$ and $B$ are *disjoint* if they have no element in common, i.e., their intersection is empty:

$$
A\cap B=∅
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets.

- Statement I is true.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\{{n}^{2}∣n\in N\} \\  & =\{1,4,9,16,…\}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}B & =\{\frac{2}{n}∣n\in N\} \\  & =\{2,1,\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{2},…\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the intersection is 

$$
\begin{aligned}A\cap B & =\{1,4,9,16,…\}\text{ }\cap \{2,1,\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{2},…\} \\  & =\{1\}. \\  & \ne ∅.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the intersection is not empty, the two sets are not disjoint.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""] ["question-37c3bc23-bd02-5d58-b8ef-2de055e363b9" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-13a24e13-db62-5670-988f-338080298b03" disjoint?

I. $\{x,y,z\}$ and $\{3,6,9\}$

II. $\{a,b,c,d,e\}$ and $\{a,e,i,o,u\}$

III. $\{1,3,6\}$ and $\{3,5,7\}$"] ["question-0803d7dd-fe65-5059-8e1e-9052cd416dca" :question/worked-solution "Two sets $A$ and $B$ are *disjoint* if they have no element in common, i.e., their intersection is empty:

$$
A\cap B=∅
$$

- Pair I is disjoint. Indeed, the intersection of the sets is empty:

$$
\{x,y,z\}\cap \{3,6,9\}=∅\,\,✓
$$

- Pair II is *not* disjoint since the intersection of the sets is not empty:

$$
\{a,b,c,d,e\}\cap \{a,e,i,o,u\}=\{a,e\}\ne ∅\,\,\times
$$

- Pair III is *not* disjoint since the intersection of the sets is not empty:

$$
\{1,3,6\}\cap \{3,5,7\}=\{3\}\ne ∅\,\,\times
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""] ["question-0803d7dd-fe65-5059-8e1e-9052cd416dca" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-d7d4f7d2-ef86-5eb2-85dd-e2f3c8149faa" ["question-4e68e4d1-4fbe-504a-90e3-9d792c948b3d" :question/math-academy-id "q-174361"] ["question-4e68e4d1-4fbe-504a-90e3-9d792c948b3d" :question/problem "Consider the following sets:

$$
A=\{n\in N∣n\le 5\},\,B=\{n\in N∣4n+6\ge 30\}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $B=\{6,7,8,…\}$

II. $A\cap B=∅$

III. $A$ and $B$ are disjoint"] ["question-4e68e4d1-4fbe-504a-90e3-9d792c948b3d" :question/worked-solution "Two sets $A$ and $B$ are *disjoint* if they have no element in common, i.e., their intersection is empty:

$$
A\cap B=∅
$$

First, notice that the elements of $B$ are positive integers that satisfy the inequality 

$$
\begin{aligned}4n+6 & \ge 30 \\ 4n & \ge 24 \\ n & \ge 6.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets.

- Statement I is true.

$$
\begin{aligned}B & =\{n\in N∣4n+6\ge 30\} \\  & =\{n\in N∣n\ge 6\} \\  & =\{6,7,8,…\}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\{n\in N∣n\le 5\} \\  & =\{1,2,3,4,5\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the intersection is 

$$
A\cap B=\{1,2,3,4,5\}\cap \{6,7,8,…\}=∅.
$$

- Statement III is true. Since the intersection is empty, the two sets are disjoint.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II and III.""] ["question-4e68e4d1-4fbe-504a-90e3-9d792c948b3d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] :question/worked-solution "Notice that the sets are overlapping since

$$
\{3,6\}\cap \{4,6\}=\{6\}\ne ∅.
$$

So, for each of our sets, we form the associated set, where each element is tagged with the corresponding index, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {A}_{1} &  & \,\to \, &  & {A}_{1}^{∗}=\{(3,1),(6,1)\} \\  & {A}_{2} &  & \,\to \, &  & {A}_{2}^{∗}=\{(4,2),(6,2)\}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the disjoint union of our sets is simply the union of the associated tagged sets:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}⊔{A}_{2} & =\{3,6\}⊔\{4,6\} \\  & ={A}_{1}^{∗}\cup {A}_{2}^{∗} \\  & =\{(3,1),(6,1)\}\cup \{(4,2),(6,2)\} \\  & =\{(3,1),(6,1),(4,2),(6,2)\}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-02e046ed-8ad2-55e9-9c98-624e899595b2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-0e822fcc-d6b3-5b6a-8dad-fa775112394a" :answer-field/id #uuid ${x}^{T}\,Ax=3.$ Given that $A$ has  eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=10$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ find the principal axes of the curve."] ["question-d4dcf09b-7fd5-51e9-80d9-32152841ce22" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=3
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{bmatrix}-10\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$"] ["question-d4dcf09b-7fd5-51e9-80d9-32152841ce22" :question/difficulty ["question-e9d96fa3-8e95-5519-8ecc-c21bd99ca106" :question/problem "Rationalize the denominator of $\frac{m}{\sqrt{m}+m}.$"] ["question-e9d96fa3-8e95-5519-8ecc-c21bd99ca106" :question/worked-solution "First, note that the denominator's conjugate is $\sqrt{m}-m.$

Now, to rationalize the denominator, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate $\sqrt{m}-m,$ and simplify:

"answer-field-856fcbb2-090f-5a4c-8cd8-b5566b8435da"] [17592186213019 :knowledge-point/questions "question-1e5c00c2-c308-529c-a13c-5c3155546628"] [17592186214235 :tutorial/content "Rationalizing the denominator works similarly for algebraic expressions as it does for numerical ones. When the denominator contains two terms and includes radicals, we multiply both the numerator and the denominator by the *conjugate* of the denominator to eliminate the radical.

For example, consider the following expression:

$$
\dfrac{1}{1+\sqrt{x}}
$$

 

To find the conjugate of the denominator $1+\sqrt{x},$ all we have to do is flip the sign between the two terms. So, the conjugate of the denominator is 

$$
1\,{\color{blue}{-}}\,\sqrt{x}.
$$

Now, to rationalize the denominator, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by $1-\sqrt{x}$ and simplify:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{1+\sqrt{x}} & = \\ \frac{1}{1+\sqrt{x}}\cdot \frac{1-\sqrt{x}}{1-\sqrt{x}} & = \\ \frac{1-\sqrt{x}}{(1+\sqrt{x})(1-\sqrt{x})} & = \\ \frac{1-\sqrt{x}}{{1}^{2}-(\sqrt{x})^{2}} & = \\ \frac{1-\sqrt{x}}{1-x}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186213279 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0]] "retractions" [[17592186060882 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a general triangle where

- side $a$ is *opposite* angle $\angle A$,
- side $b$ is *opposite* angle $\angle B$, and
- side $c$ is *opposite* angle $\angle C$,

as follows:

![](images/8f/8f3d3bf4824508ef152e8d8d567672d7d61fb36e0ffb533d97be7294e9198956.png)

The **law of cosines** states that

$$
\begin{aligned}
a^{2} &= b^{2} + c^{2} - 2bc\cos A \\
b^{2} &= a^{2} + c^{2} - 2ac\cos B \\
c^{2} &= a^{2} + b^{2} - 2ab\cos C
\end{aligned}
$$

We can use this to calculate the length of one side when we know two sides and one angle.

If we look at the law of cosines we see that it's quite similar to the Pythagorean theorem:

$$
a^2+b^2=c^2
$$

But remember that the Pythagorean theorem can *only* be used for a *right-angled triangle*!

![](images/db/db9ed4aac9ca46ffc95d393d863cb09e9ba874caf0008410937f961fdf6c7ab6.png)

The law of cosines is more general and can be used on *any* triangle.

**Note:** To remember the law of cosines, it's helpful to notice that the equations always follow the same pattern:

$$
(side opposite; the angle)^{2} = (adjacent; side)^{2} + (adjacent; other side)^{2} - 2(adjacent; side)(adjacent; other side)\cos (angle)
$$

We'll show how this formula can be derived at the end of the lesson."] [17592186060884 :tutorial/content "Let's look at our general triangle again.

![](images/8f/8f3d3bf4824508ef152e8d8d567672d7d61fb36e0ffb533d97be7294e9198956.png)

When we know the lengths of three sides of a triangle, we rearrange the law of cosines to find an angle:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a^{2} &= b^{2} + c^{2} - 2bc\cos A \\
2bc\cos A &= b^{2} + c^{2} - a^{2} \\
\cos A &= \frac{b^{2} + c^{2} - a^{2}}{2bc}
\end{aligned}
$$

So, for all the angles, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos A &= \frac{b^{2} + c^{2} - a^{2}}{2bc}, \\
\cos B &= \frac{a^{2} + c^{2} - b^{2}}{2ac}, \\
\cos C &= \frac{a^{2} + b^{2} - c^{2}}{2ab}
\end{aligned}
$$

It's helpful to notice that the equations always follow the same pattern:

$$
\cos (angle) = ((adjacent; side)^{2} + (adjacent; other side)^{2} - (side opposite; the angle)^{2})/(2(adjacent; side)(adjacent; other side))
$$"] [17592186060863 :tutorial/content "Let's now derive the law of cosines in the following form:

$$
a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A
$$

Consider $\triangle ABC$ with sides of lengths $a,b$, and $c$, as shown below.

![](images/7c/7cc2a0cbb6a02af829e070fc54cfdbe616683f86527b119a530053a34048e699.png)

Let's now add the height $\overline{CH}$ and assume it has length $h$, as shown.

![](images/d4/d4e80b2b54283ea353b687d959e9d8fc6c9303e85081c0a46b48703ee3dae7d5.png)

The remainder of this proof consists of two steps:

- **Step 1**: Write down expressions for $\cos A$ and $\sin A$.
- **Step 2**: Apply the Pythagorean theorem to $\triangle BHC$, and simplify.

Using elementary trigonometry, we have

$$
\cos A = \dfrac{AH}{b}, \qquad \sin A = \dfrac{h}{b}
$$

which can be written as

$$
AH = b\cos A, \qquad h = b\sin A
$$

Applying the Pythagorean theorem to $\triangle BHC$ and using our expression for $h$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
a^{2} &= (BH)^{2} + h^{2} \\
a^{2} &= (BH)^{2} + b^{2}\sin^{2} A
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the length of the side $\overline{AB}$. Since $\overline{AB}$ consists of two segments, $\overline{AH}$ and $\overline{BH}$, we have

$$
c = AH + BH\quad \Longrightarrow\quad BH = c - AH
$$

and using our expression for $AH$, we have

$$
BH = c - b\cos A
$$

Substituting this into our expression for $a^2$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
a^{2} &= (BH)^{2} + b^{2}\sin^{2} A \\
&= (c - b\cos A)^{2} + b^{2}\sin^{2} A \\
&= c^{2} - 2bc\cos A + b^{2}\cos^{2} A + b^{2}\sin^{2} A \\
&= b^{2}\cos^{2} A + b^{2}\sin^{2} A + c^{2} - 2bc\cos A \\
&= b^{2}(\cos^{2} A + \sin^{2} A) + c^{2} - 2bc\cos A
\end{aligned}
$$

It can be shown that

$$
\cos^2A + \sin^2 A = 1
$$

for any angle $A$ (this is the Pythagorean theorem in trigonometric form). Therefore, we have

$$
a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A
$$

as required.

$$"] [17592186060905 :tutorial/content "A **quadrantal angle** is an angle whose terminal side lies on the $x$ or $y$-axis.

$$

in radians.

$$

When the denominator contains two terms and includes radicals, we multiply both the numerator and the denominator by the *conjugate* of the denominator to eliminate the radical.

For example, consider the following expression:

$$
\dfrac{1}{1+\sqrt{x}}
$$

To find the conjugate of the denominator $1+\sqrt{x}$, all we have to do is flip the sign between the two terms. So, the conjugate of the denominator is

$$
1\,{\color{blue}{-}}\,\sqrt{x}
$$

Now, to rationalize the denominator, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by $1-\sqrt{x}$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{x}} &=  \\
\frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{x}} \cdot \frac{1 - \sqrt{x}}{1 - \sqrt{x}} &=  \\
(1 - \sqrt{x})/((1 + \sqrt{x})(1 - \sqrt{x})) &=  \\
(1 - \sqrt{x})/(1^{2} - (\sqrt{x})^{2}) &=  \\
&= \frac{1 - \sqrt{x}}{1 - x}
\end{aligned}

Consider the system of linear ODEs and two of its linearly independent solutions ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ shown above. Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?" :question/worked-solution "Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2t \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}=\begin{bmatrix}2t{e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$

$$

$$

Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the {{field-1}} of {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line {{field-4}} by the properties of determinants." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L1}.$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the $\text{columns}$ of $Φ,$ namely the functions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ These functions are the fundamental solutions of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Recall that a matrix has linearly independent columns if and only if its determinant is nonzero. Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for any particular $t,$

$$
det(Φ(t))\ne 0.
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by the properties of determinants."} {:db/id 17592186221422 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221192 :question/id #uuid </tr></tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(2t)={e}^{2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(2t)={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
2t{e}^{2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(1-2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2{e}^{2t}t+{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\  & ={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{2t}t \\  & =t{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186221989 :question/id #uuid "5ca7cf8a-29b9-5dc9-9eb7-2eb98441be57" :question/math-academy-id "q-333713"} {:db/id 17592186308497 :question/id #uuid "eff0b088-3db3-5966-a1d7-4ea54d40635c" :question/math-academy-id "q-333715" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e2ca6901-556b-5960-a3bd-8d0552587579" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186307252}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186307252} :answer-field/id #uuid "09352193-2085-5ed0-9dac-3b45c1b2f367" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307553} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2961f6c2-30e1-5479-98d1-86e05fd1e48e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186305541}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186305541} :answer-field/id #uuid "743ad797-c4e6-5a90-81e7-9503d1668174" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307887}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "$$

The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-2t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-2t) &={e}^{-2t} \\ r(2t) &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-2t} \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtraction the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-4t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}-{e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-2t}-{e}^{2t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}) \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2\cdot (-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-4t}-{e}^{4t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308609 :question/id #uuid "64533ce4-1ae9-513d-ba89-484c2cf3a62c" :question/math-academy-id "q-334382" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5d8223f6-d576-5e04-89fc-1464abef50dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{sin}(5t)" :db/id 17592186306050}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186306050} :answer-field/id #uuid "0cae7130-92fe-567b-b98b-6f508a21ed99" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307569} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c3417787-0b37-54ba-b621-e6d55ac43b3d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}(5t)" :db/id 17592186306971}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186306971} :answer-field/id #uuid "5c20d515-1f48-5aec-946c-716105bcbbf0" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307810} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "dfed4f33-2d1f-51a1-a259-d0e2ac8c0f8d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}(5t)" :db/id 17592186307224}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186307224} :answer-field/id #uuid "e6a5f5a6-0b5f-5445-b33d-5f25bda05525" :answer-field/key "field-4" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186308251} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "057dc0c1-9b91-5408-bfb2-87575fdd4609" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}(5t)" :db/id 17592186305200}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186305200} :answer-field/id #uuid "f8d91ade-2020-5dea-8c9b-3e7b3560fbbb" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186308313}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |

|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-5\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((5\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(5\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(5\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+5\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & =5\cdot \frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308611 :question/id #uuid "ff10c64d-19c8-5825-958b-92dcd06d6e53" :question/math-academy-id "q-334387" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b642857-d5c7-5354-9582-e84b796c8d0c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}" :db/id 17592186305568}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186305568} :answer-field/id #uuid "191d5551-a712-5140-91a3-ad273a6ad519" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307600} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bfdf9ccd-6d68-52b8-90d2-de98adb98891" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}" :db/id 17592186306941}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186306941} :answer-field/id #uuid "69784144-c83c-5567-a773-771397a8e2ee" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307859}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "$$

$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

$$

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365668 :question/id #uuid "162963ac-9899-549d-9b3f-b09605170db6" :question/math-academy-id "q-334389"} {:db/id 17592186365673 :question/id #uuid "93c5b9c1-d3c4-52c5-af95-03ae43585aaf" :question/math-academy-id "q-334497" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5728e179-6831-5401-a928-e641db0a06b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{-4t}" :db/id 17592186365675}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365675} :answer-field/id #uuid "afbc2e57-8b1b-5ce4-9b27-cb6cab8bfe1d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365674} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "979acb26-7ddd-5b55-9211-9925729aa071" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186365677}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365677} :answer-field/id #uuid "43739f8d-9cc2-5a3f-8f44-3fd681edf8db" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365676} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8029db2d-8bde-50dd-9836-f39ca854a3bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t{e}^{-4t}" :db/id 17592186365679}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365679} :answer-field/id #uuid "faaddf78-a1db-5496-a708-d82d0e79d47b" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365678} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6356927b-4df6-547a-97be-5637f834898e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{-4t}" :db/id 17592186365681}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365681} :answer-field/id #uuid "c911bdd1-5a68-53a2-90c8-77d2d0783bc8" :answer-field/key "field-4" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365680}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(4t) &={e}^{4t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{4t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{4t} \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186534093 :question/id #uuid "f69ba2b0-76ef-5087-a5bf-906e0adf24a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-334388" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a54e01d-d3da-520d-a71e-fb2b3d3a8bd9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{6t}+e^{-6t}" :db/id 17592186533275}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186533275} :answer-field/id #uuid "1ec158fd-889b-5066-b795-fdf52e06926c" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186533801} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f40c120d-2ef8-574c-b604-70f11f9600d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{6t}+e^{-6t}" :db/id 17592186533740}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186533740} :answer-field/id #uuid "5ac691a2-04d5-52ef-bc49-8d3327cd84e3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186533851}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "$$

</tr></tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-6t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=6t,
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-6t)={e}^{-6t} \\ r(6t)={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t} \\ 6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-12t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot (-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} \\ {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186558512 :question/id #uuid "4c0f5df5-2d8b-5cef-a048-d87044456178" :question/math-academy-id "q-334464" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2aa1a93d-75a0-5e01-ae23-5b0f8e1ac112" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186557956}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186557956} :answer-field/id #uuid "2ae25ef7-c29f-5097-8973-b2adfaba1611" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186558377} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "37b1d3e9-bd96-5587-a427-f6db2fe1f661" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{2t}" :db/id 17592186557980}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186557980} :answer-field/id #uuid "7820253f-f186-5cf9-9944-b249ef50c9a8" :answer-field/key "field-4" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186558416} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a08282a0-0997-5c3f-ac2d-158a5280db4a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186558184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186558184} :answer-field/id #uuid "bccb1e87-298a-5c8e-ae6e-cd3c1dfaaf2b" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186558449} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e9a7c02c-3d69-5ee9-b2d1-6e74980ea60e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{-t}" :db/id 17592186558337}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186558337} :answer-field/id #uuid "cc546b2a-f18f-5a02-9cc9-a4dfb2de1de2" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186558455}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=2t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-t)={e}^{-t} \\ r(2t)={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-t} \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{-t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-\frac{{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{-t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{-t} \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2\cdot \frac{{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{-t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186558572 :question/id #uuid "e2ad2fef-a91c-56d1-9362-f2fbd4a52e56" :question/math-academy-id "q-334463" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1aec3636-0b05-53aa-b49f-bb68ba34e051" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{5t}" :db/id 17592186557927}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186557927} :answer-field/id #uuid "46deef4f-e56b-5e36-8314-39c65e6b0ff6" :answer-field/key "field-4" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186558385} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0f82863e-1510-5b78-bcdf-021a61eb750f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186557898}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186557898} :answer-field/id #uuid "964568c1-49f6-591e-9282-96ed07b39888" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186558431} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4742a9e2-e4be-5551-9318-6d3fbbd26726" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{2t}" :db/id 17592186558007}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186558007} :answer-field/id #uuid "beaac546-5dc7-52af-aedb-cbfc055afecd" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186558452} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ad67dc0e-85fd-5faa-84ba-66c09b001f9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186558211}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186558211} :answer-field/id #uuid "e9189462-1f98-510b-b2f5-d3d5e93103dc" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186558470}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=5t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(2t)={e}^{2t} \\ r(5t)={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t} \\ 5t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{2t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{5{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{5t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2t\cdot \frac{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{2t}}{3t}+\frac{5{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{5t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{2t} \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5t\cdot \frac{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{2t}}{3t}+\frac{5{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{5t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048231} {:activity/expected-seconds 960.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186222332} :activity/id #uuid "bf2387fe-ebed-5568-a260-0d681cb9fd28" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050228 :topic/id #uuid "37d183d8-ce59-581c-9a89-fec7544aae03" :topic/math-academy-id 6376} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186222332 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222502 :tutorial/content "Consider the homogeneous linear system

$$
\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x},
$$

where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix.

A **fundamental matrix** for this system is an $n\times n$ matrix $\Phi(t)$ whose columns are $n$ linearly independent solutions of the system.

If $\mathbf{x}_1(t),\dots,\mathbf{x}_n(t)$ are linearly independent solutions, then one fundamental matrix is

$$
\Phi(t)=\big[\mathbf{x}_1(t),\dots,\mathbf{x}_n(t)\big].
$$

**Note:** The columns of $\Phi(t)$ can be written in any order.

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "a7207a24-194d-59d6-b25c-f9bb4f1b0d6e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14508 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3b0bd285-b383-5ebb-821f-4f74a0b37719" :step/math-academy-id 594316 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222333}} {:db/id 17592186222333 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221420 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221191 :question/id #uuid "4874a486-2cf1-5b6e-ae4f-52579f03b077" :question/math-academy-id "e-21695"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "af871f3d-da9e-5fd3-a61f-94e155ccf2b3" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049851}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221985} {:db/id 17592186221999} {:db/id 17592186308599} {:db/id 17592186308600} {:db/id 17592186308601} {:db/id 17592186398781} {:db/id 17592186442556} {:db/id 17592186442557} {:db/id 17592186442562} {:db/id 17592186558553}] :knowledge-point/title "Constructing a Fundamental Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "aa3c7790-3ab9-5519-bad3-4f82fc8ac113" :step/math-academy-id 594317 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222334}} {:db/id 17592186222334 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222503 :tutorial/content "Again, let $\Phi(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for the linear system

$$
\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x},
$$

where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix. The fundamental matrices have the following important properties.

1\. *Satisfies the underlying system*. Indeed, since each column of $\Phi(t)$ is a solution of the system, we have

  $$
  \Phi'(t) = A\,\Phi(t).
  $$

2\. *Invertibility*. The columns of $\Phi(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t,$ so

  $$
  \det\Phi(t)\neq 0
  $$

  for all $t.$ In particular, $\Phi(t)$ is invertible for all $t.$

3\. *Representation of solutions*. Every solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ of the system can be written in the form

  $$
  \mathbf{x}(t)=\Phi(t)\,\mathbf{c},
  $$

  where $\mathbf{c}$ is a constant vector.

4\. *Non-uniqueness*. If $C$ is any invertible constant matrix, then

  $$
  \Psi(t)=\Phi(t)\,C
  $$

  is also a fundamental matrix for the same system.

We'll now get some practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "e2fdbc29-4542-5fdc-adbd-316c5dcb6878" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14509 :tutorial/title "Properties of the Fundamental Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "2fe7252e-7fc7-59bb-bc32-74c452b7cf73" :step/math-academy-id 594320 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222335}} {:db/id 17592186222335 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221421 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221193 :question/id #uuid "a52a6539-60d1-557c-a042-cbce5616e94f" :question/math-academy-id "e-21697"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0aea7503-74d6-5ba4-9411-ee53e59512d0" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221990} {:db/id 17592186221991} {:db/id 17592186311648} {:db/id 17592186311687} {:db/id 17592186365731} {:db/id 17592186391264} {:db/id 17592186396895} {:db/id 17592186396916} {:db/id 17592186442561} {:db/id 17592186498522} {:db/id 17592186498584} {:db/id 17592186533984}] :knowledge-point/title "Proving Properties of a Fundamental Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "2b90cd12-9695-5b6b-b407-6eed6ae7fc84" :step/math-academy-id 594321 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222336}} {:db/id 17592186222336 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222504 :tutorial/content "For a linear system $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ with constant $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ the **standard fundamental matrix** is the unique fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ that satisfies the initial condition

$$
\Phi_0(0)=I_n,
$$

where $I_n$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix.

For constant matrices $A,$ the standard fundamental matrix is given by

$$
\Phi_0(t)=e^{At}.
$$

This matrix satisfies

$$
\Phi_0'(t)=A\,\Phi_0(t)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\Phi_0(0)=I_n.
$$

**Note:** Any other fundamental matrix $\Phi(t)$ for the same system can be written in the form

$$
\Phi(t)=\Phi_0(t)\,C,

$$
\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x},
$$

where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix. The fundamental matrices have the following important properties.

1\. *Satisfies the underlying system*. Indeed, since each column of $\Phi(t)$ is a solution of the system, we have

  $$
  \Phi'(t) = A\,\Phi(t).
  $$

2\. *Invertibility*. The columns of $\Phi(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t,$ so

  $$
  \det\Phi(t)\neq 0
  $$

  for all $t.$ In particular, $\Phi(t)$ is invertible for all $t.$

3\. *Representation of solutions*. Every solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ of the system can be written in the form

  $$
  \mathbf{x}(t)=\Phi(t)\,\mathbf{c},
  $$

  where $\mathbf{c}$ is a constant vector.

4\. *Non-uniqueness*. If $C$ is any invertible constant matrix, then

  $$
  \Psi(t)=\Phi(t)\,C
  $$

  is also a fundamental matrix for the same system.

$$
\Phi_0(0)=I_n,
$$

where $I_n$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix.

For constant matrices $A,$ the standard fundamental matrix is given by

$$
\Phi_0(t)=e^{At}.
$$

This matrix satisfies

$$
\Phi_0'(t)=A\,\Phi_0(t)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\Phi_0(0)=I_n.
$$

**Note:** Any other fundamental matrix $\Phi(t)$ for the same system can be written in the form

$$
\Phi(t)=\Phi_0(t)\,C,
$$

where $C$ is an invertible constant matrix.

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=7t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(4t) &={e}^{4t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{4t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{4t} \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3ad30acf-66b9-5977-ad36-2183bb8c58c8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186498619}} {:db/id 17592186498623 :step/content {:db/id 17592186365659 :question/answer-fields $$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3ea51f6a-6ea8-5162-ad6a-900689393007" :step/next {:db/id 17592186498620}} {:db/id 17592186498653 :step/content {:db/id 17592186498584 :question/answer-fields {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d656b9e3-27c9-51a6-a70f-c9d56643be83" :question/math-academy-id "q-336108" :question/problem "Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-3}} by the transitive property of equality." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives $x(t)=Φ(t)c.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3 and L4}.$"} :step/id #uuid We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives $x(t)=Φ(t)c.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3 and L4}.$"} :step/id #uuid $\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

{:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "3f77715c-0903-5f4b-a449-6816c6d9bb06" :question/math-academy-id "q-334465" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

<table align="l" cellpadding="0" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="40px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="40px">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center"></td>
<td align="center">{{field-3}}</td>
<td align="center" width="30px">{{field-4}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=7t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(4t) &={e}^{4t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{4t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{4t} \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3ad30acf-66b9-5977-ad36-2183bb8c58c8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186498619}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "dae93f70-eae4-559e-a461-fdfe0abd280a" :answer/type {:db/id "20281150-3bf1-5302-a5be-765695a3b8d8" :question/math-academy-id "q-336094" :question/problem "Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the {{field-1}} of {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line {{field-4}} by the properties of determinants." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L1}.$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the $\text{columns}$ of $Φ,$ namely the functions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ These functions are the fundamental solutions of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Recall that a matrix has linearly independent columns if and only if its determinant is nonzero. Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for any particular $t,$

$$
det(Φ(t))\ne 0.
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by the properties of determinants."} :step/id #uuid "231eb329-513b-5dfb-85da-6e0f13afe8fd"} {:db/id 17592186534111 :step/content {:db/id 17592186398781 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7c007ca0-acef-5af6-b3fe-264373817071" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-1} & 2{e}^{-1} \\ 0 & {e}^{-1}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186398783} {:answer/id #uuid "59ce7ec4-615c-508f-9c8e-4b5a5d18d797" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 2t{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186398784} {:answer/id #uuid "b333daa7-d3c9-5885-83dd-c52477a27945" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2t \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186398785} {:answer/id #uuid "1281b7c7-c44e-5d28-ae85-689e0d3ae235" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} & 2t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186398786} {:answer/id #uuid "de8dcb0a-6338-525e-8932-5efde71571f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186398787}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186398786} :answer-field/id #uuid "f91e0298-1d33-5125-a1ef-22a1c3b27757" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186398782}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "6ce970ec-3f9d-57d6-9307-1253ccd1b689" :question/math-academy-id "q-334326" :question/problem "$$

Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?" :question/worked-solution "Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2t \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}=\begin{bmatrix}2t{e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} & 2t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order."} :step/id #uuid "24523b4e-4e57-53cd-8b40-7f56c7c2589e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534142}} {:db/id 17592186534127 :step/content {:db/id
