17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7179862e-a345-5508-93d4-73732015d190" :question/math-academy-id "q-333723" :question/problem "Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & -4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-4t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-4t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
-4t{e}^{-4t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}(1+4t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-4{e}^{-4t}t+{e}^{-4t}(1+4t) \\  & ={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{-4t}t \\  & =t{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t} & t{e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6372c740-c40b-54b4-b2d8-d67db30bf1d4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534109}} {:db/id 17592186534142 :step/content {:db/id 17592186534093 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a54e01d-d3da-520d-a71e-fb2b3d3a8bd9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{6t}+e^{-6t}" :db/id 17592186533275}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186533275} :answer-field/id #uuid "1ec158fd-889b-5066-b795-fdf52e06926c" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186533801} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f40c120d-2ef8-574c-b604-70f11f9600d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{6t}+e^{-6t}" :db/id 17592186533740}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186533740} :answer-field/id #uuid "5ac691a2-04d5-52ef-bc49-8d3327cd84e3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186533851}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "f69ba2b0-76ef-5087-a5bf-906e0adf24a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-334388" :question/problem "$$

</tr></tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-6t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=6t,
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-6t)={e}^{-6t} \\ r(6t)={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t} \\ 6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-12t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot (-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} \\ {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}\end{aligned}].
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a9bd7aaf-ed47-5adf-8e37-bc1f645e1959" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534128}}] :activity/title "Fundamental Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$"} :step/id #uuid "62363ed1-22ab-56fa-9971-8c017f526c79" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534111}} {:db/id system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line {{field-4}} by the properties of determinants." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Recall that a matrix has linearly independent columns if and only if its determinant is nonzero. Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for any particular $t,$

Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?" :question/worked-solution "Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2t \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}=\begin{bmatrix}2t{e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} & 2t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order."} :step/id #uuid "24523b4e-4e57-53cd-8b40-7f56c7c2589e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534142}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid :question/math-academy-id "q-334388" :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

<table align="l" cellpadding="0" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="80px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="80px">${e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t}$</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center"></td>
<td align="center" width="80px">${e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t}$</td>
<td align="center" width="80px">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr></tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-6t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=6t,
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-6t)={e}^{-6t} \\ r(6t)={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t} \\ 6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-12t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot (-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} \\ {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}\end{aligned}].
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a9bd7aaf-ed47-5adf-8e37-bc1f645e1959" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534128}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3b918900-9d47-501a-8fe9-03921f6ed92d" :answer/type {:db/id A=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & -4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-4t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-4t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
-4t{e}^{-4t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}(1+4t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-4{e}^{-4t}t+{e}^{-4t}(1+4t) \\  & ={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{-4t}t \\  & =t{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t} & t{e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6372c740-c40b-54b4-b2d8-d67db30bf1d4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534109}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5728e179-6831-5401-a928-e641db0a06b5" :answer/type {:db/id A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | ${e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | ${e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}$ | {{field-2}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-3t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-3t) &={e}^{-3t} \\ r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-3t} \\ 3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-6t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}) \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & =3\cdot (-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t} \\ {e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "64943c28-d0a3-53a2-88a5-d9adefa020e7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186546015}} {:db/id 17592186545970 :step/content {:db/id 17592186365731 :question/answer-fields "9e4b9ffe-ff7e-5035-97f0-e9cfaaf038a3" :question/math-academy-id "q-336308" :question/problem "Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ satisfies the matrix differential equation ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A\,Φ(t)$ is given below.

*Hint: $[a,\,b]$ denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors $a$ and $b.$*

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[{x}_{1}^{′}(t),\,{x}_{2}^{′}(t)]$

$\text{L5}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[A{x}_{1}(t),\,A{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t)$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L4}$ and substitution from lines {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ and substitution from line {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider line $\text{L3}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent solutions of the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t).$ This means that each column satisfies the differential equation. In particular, 

$$
{x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that ${x}_{2}\text{ is a solution of the system}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L5}.$ By definition, the derivative of $Φ(t)$ is obtained by differentiating each column,

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}^{′}(t) & {x}_{2}^{′}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$ from $\text{L3},$ we substitute each derivative into the matrix to get

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ A{x}_{1}(t) & A{x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substitution from $\text{L2}\text{ and }\text{L3}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ From $\text{L6}$ we have

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)].
$$

Using the definition $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$ from $\text{L1},$ we substitute to obtain

$$

The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-5\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((5\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(5\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(5\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+5\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & =5\cdot \frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c739f31a-33e2-5b79-9d44-a58e2e368af7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186545937}} {:db/id 17592186545985 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221988 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4475a7f4-c95c-5c55-8109-0e9ea886a2a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186545329}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186545329} :answer-field/id #uuid "aa786690-2dc1-59f3-a44d-639db8237f3d" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186220583} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10f335ea-9d53-5bd8-a277-0e71096d1701" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{2t}" :db/id 17592186545230}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186545230} :answer-field/id #uuid "ee77c4e2-6eb2-5db9-8618-4ba0d57d6223" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186220584} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d4192bd6-a9b5-5e3c-a850-538acc11b68f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{2t}" :db/id 17592186545587}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186545587} :answer-field/id #uuid "4f7022e0-ee16-5d5b-b4f3-9eb2d8be983b" :answer-field/key "field-4" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186220585} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "227c788b-a841-56fc-9c67-21ee4721d3f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "te^{2t}" :db/id 17592186545272}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186545272} :answer-field/id #uuid "7c1b35ed-a68f-5e20-b0c8-7a1d98ca67ae" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186220586}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d2008090-84f9-50fd-9af0-82b54be4b43f" :question/math-academy-id "q-333712" :question/problem "$$

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.

A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | ${e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | ${e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}$ | {{field-2}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-3t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-3t) &={e}^{-3t} \\ r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-3t} \\ 3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-6t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}) \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & =3\cdot (-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t} \\ {e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "64943c28-d0a3-53a2-88a5-d9adefa020e7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186546015}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b642857-d5c7-5354-9582-e84b796c8d0c" :answer/type {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-334382" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-5\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((5\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(5\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(5\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+5\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & =5\cdot \frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c739f31a-33e2-5b79-9d44-a58e2e368af7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186545937}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5d8223f6-d576-5e04-89fc-1464abef50dd" :answer/type {:db/id </tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=5t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(2t)={e}^{2t} \\ r(5t)={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t} \\ 5t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{2t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{5{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{5t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2t\cdot \frac{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{2t}}{3t}+\frac{5{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{5t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{2t} \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5t\cdot \frac{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{2t}}{3t}+\frac{5{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{5t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].
$$"} :step/id #uuid "20da1ed7-1f0c-5835-8b4d-dcc25234e0b0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186558602}} {:db/id 17592186558602 :step/content {:db/id 17592186558512 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2aa1a93d-75a0-5e01-ae23-5b0f8e1ac112" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186557956}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186557956} :answer-field/id #uuid "2ae25ef7-c29f-5097-8973-b2adfaba1611" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186558377} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "37b1d3e9-bd96-5587-a427-f6db2fe1f661" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{2t}" :db/id 17592186557980}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186557980} :answer-field/id #uuid "7820253f-f186-5cf9-9944-b249ef50c9a8" :answer-field/key "field-4" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186558416} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a08282a0-0997-5c3f-ac2d-158a5280db4a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186558184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186558184} :answer-field/id #uuid "bccb1e87-298a-5c8e-ae6e-cd3c1dfaaf2b" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186558449} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e9a7c02c-3d69-5ee9-b2d1-6e74980ea60e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{-t}" :db/id 17592186558337}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186558337} :answer-field/id #uuid "cc546b2a-f18f-5a02-9cc9-a4dfb2de1de2" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186558455}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "4c0f5df5-2d8b-5cef-a048-d87044456178" :question/math-academy-id "q-334464" :question/problem "$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=2t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-t)={e}^{-t} \\ r(2t)={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-t} \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{-t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-\frac{{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{-t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{-t} \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2\cdot \frac{{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{-t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$"} :step/id #uuid "28175361-001a-5814-a2f8-5b17cada3b66" :step/next {:db/id 17592186558640}} {:db/id 17592186558604 :step/content {:db/id 17592186308497 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e2ca6901-556b-5960-a3bd-8d0552587579" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186307252}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186307252} :answer-field/id #uuid "09352193-2085-5ed0-9dac-3b45c1b2f367" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307553} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2961f6c2-30e1-5479-98d1-86e05fd1e48e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186305541}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186305541} :answer-field/id #uuid "743ad797-c4e6-5a90-81e7-9503d1668174" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307887}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "eff0b088-3db3-5966-a1d7-4ea54d40635c" :question/math-academy-id "q-333715" :question/problem "$$

The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-2t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-2t) &={e}^{-2t} \\ r(2t) &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-2t} \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtraction the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-4t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}-{e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-2t}-{e}^{2t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}) \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2\cdot (-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-4t}-{e}^{4t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2d713ccf-e8ff-5322-acfc-63ee36bee9c3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186558662}} {:db/id 17592186558640 :step/content {:db/id 17592186308634 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c339771-09ba-5022-9518-b108d54d7a85" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t{e}^{5t}" :db/id 17592186305572}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186305572} :answer-field/id #uuid "3dd870b2-a7c5-5395-803e-55ce4d4f4943" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307713} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a803fbc-355e-5705-83ad-dd81e32fcabc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186305395}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186305395} :answer-field/id #uuid "4f6b70cd-fe87-553d-9371-7a3f6e38337f" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307763} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "cbc416a2-fcf3-5f9c-b6c8-072133cbba6c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{5t}" :db/id 17592186307041}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186307041} :answer-field/id #uuid "78b8505f-4ff7-51cd-8b58-a89db40093f8" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307902} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6f7fee4a-c580-56e8-ad35-f8a8f1d5812e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{5t}" :db/id 17592186306213}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186306213} :answer-field/id #uuid "f547f3a4-4a17-530c-9994-4e346ffc2d43" :answer-field/key "field-4" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186308298}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "691520cf-4380-50be-8b5c-ac8a181c7472" :question/math-academy-id "q-334499" :question/problem "$$

The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & 5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(5t) &={e}^{5t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(5t) &={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}5t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{5t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{5t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
5t{e}^{5t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t}(1-5t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5{e}^{5t}t+{e}^{5t}(1-5t) \\  & ={e}^{5t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{5t}t \\  & =t{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "711a72fe-d404-510a-8960-ed2ab6a98eaa"} {:db/id 17592186558662 :step/content {:db/id 17592186558553 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "50015ef5-0e92-5106-aea9-ab330a93796e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186558019} {:answer/id #uuid "b590d98d-384a-59d4-bdd6-f31990d7de3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{2t} & {e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t} & 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186558229} {:answer/id #uuid "c4fd659a-e0ec-5349-a757-959b558799ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186558261} {:answer/id #uuid "d8a149ea-0805-59fc-962e-46dd8b99f2a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}1 & t \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186558294} {:answer/id #uuid "e5478b07-ac20-593b-879f-47d35b336561" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2} & {e}^{2} \\ 0 & {e}^{2}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186558324}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186558261} :answer-field/id #uuid "543370ed-7818-5d7f-878c-1a15d0e76c82" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186558397}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a83f3a56-7f37-59d6-8ed6-dd0cc81608ee" :question/math-academy-id "q-334302" :question/problem "$$

Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?" :question/worked-solution "Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}=[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order."} :step/id #uuid "9b0e4e07-3c1a-5e15-8966-efc4693d635c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186558595}}] :activity/title "Fundamental Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186557860} {:db/id 17592186046669} {:db/id 17592186558604 :step/content {:db/id 17592186308497 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e2ca6901-556b-5960-a3bd-8d0552587579" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186307252}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186307252} :answer-field/id #uuid "09352193-2085-5ed0-9dac-3b45c1b2f367" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307553} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2961f6c2-30e1-5479-98d1-86e05fd1e48e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186305541}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186305541} :answer-field/id #uuid "743ad797-c4e6-5a90-81e7-9503d1668174" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307887}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "eff0b088-3db3-5966-a1d7-4ea54d40635c" :question/math-academy-id "q-333715" :question/problem "$$

$$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{5t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
5t{e}^{5t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t}(1-5t).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5{e}^{5t}t+{e}^{5t}(1-5t) \\  & ={e}^{5t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{5t}t \\  & =t{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?" :question/worked-solution "Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}=[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order."} :step/id #uuid "9b0e4e07-3c1a-5e15-8966-efc4693d635c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186558595}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid So, we can keep subtracting $4$ from the input until we get to an input that we see in the graph:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(62) & =f(62-4) \\  & =f(62-2\cdot 4) \\  & =⋯ \\  & =f(62-15\cdot 4) \\  & =f(2) \\  & =0\end{aligned}

simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-x=-5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }0\,\text{d}t \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180040 :question/id #uuid "4edd3b9a-070a-593a-8f84-1b14657d2c07" :question/math-academy-id "q-127055" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179744 :knowledge-point/id #uuid where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x+y=3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t), \\ Q(x,y) & =y-x=3(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t))\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(3(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t))\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1\,\text{d}t \\  & =9t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =9(2\pi -0) \\  & =18\pi \end{aligned}

$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(9{cos}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{1}^{1}(u+{u}^{3})\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(49{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(1)\cdot (-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98{cos}^{3}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-98{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{0}-98{u}^{2}\,du \\  & =(98\operatorname{sin}⁡t-7\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=8\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.

$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(32\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(24\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-8\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }192({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }192\,\text{d}t \\  & =192t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =192(2\pi -0) \\  & =384\pi \end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={e}^{y}={e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t}, \\ Q(x,y) & ={e}^{x}={e}^{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({e}^{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}{e}^{u}\,du-{\int }_{1}^{1}{e}^{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =0\end{aligned}

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{3}=8{sin}^{3}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =2+x=2+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,du=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(8{sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(2+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t+16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{0}16{u}^{3}+16u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t{|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}=4{sin}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-xy=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt=du,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }6\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}6{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}

$$

$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=8\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the double-angle formula for cosine, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (8\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(\frac{1}{4})\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }32{cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }32(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1}{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+16t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =(0+32\pi -1)-(0-1) \\  & =32\pi \end{aligned}

17592186262334}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=7\,i+2\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=36.$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $6.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =7, \\ Q(x,y) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(7)\cdot (6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(2)\cdot (-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }42\operatorname{cos}⁡t+12\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(42\operatorname{sin}⁡t-12\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =(0-12)-(0-12) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186262716 :question/id #uuid "79c34a7b-b623-515b-8476-bf469364ea95" :question/math-academy-id "q-127143" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a1393ce9-919a-5a3f-a8c5-3ce471d06ed6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186261276} {:answer/id #uuid "a40cd9e0-094a-53e2-bea7-72696c9a5f5c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186261304} {:answer/id #uuid "a5d88754-afb8-5215-960d-6c87c992d632" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186261315} {:answer/id #uuid "c6e3c02b-04d6-59c7-b162-6bd0c1725f86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186261634} {:answer/id #uuid "c73cd479-dfcc-5a7b-abdd-2aab64decf0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186261638}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186261638} :answer-field/id #uuid "f19e243a-d229-55b5-b933-2f21b1dc4b86" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262543}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{3}\,i+{x}^{3}\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={1}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $1.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{3}={sin}^{3}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{3}={cos}^{3}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({cos}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t({sin}^{2}+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186262717 :question/id #uuid "f3f2013e-6c87-5135-8bb8-8a0a551136de" :question/math-academy-id "q-127144"} {:db/id 17592186262718 :question/id #uuid "bf94cd2c-9106-5cc5-9f8f-bee0a724f45f" :question/math-academy-id "q-127145"} {:db/id 17592186262719 :question/id #uuid "07fc4782-ce17-55e6-b2c6-9fdd11a42eea" :question/math-academy-id "q-127146"} {:db/id 17592186262720 :question/id #uuid "4b077b66-1e99-5133-b08d-623645791b05" :question/math-academy-id "q-127148"} {:db/id 17592186262721 :question/id #uuid "5660b13f-68bb-56f7-8d7c-83ccf48f3c64" :question/math-academy-id "q-127149" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6d6e8dc0-de0b-5246-baf1-2e88a94ead89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "25\pi " :db/id 17592186260835} {:answer/id #uuid "86aa0ca4-2fef-5ea7-ab52-7326ec1150e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-75\pi " :db/id 17592186261048} {:answer/id #uuid "945c2bc9-3eea-5671-ac58-7ea3e0a8ed17" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "150\pi " :db/id 17592186261168} {:answer/id #uuid "b7033798-e10d-5128-ab9b-7bc561366c39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-100\pi " :db/id 17592186261481} {:answer/id #uuid "dcaaf559-e7cf-5424-90bb-d31bc261f4d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "50\pi " :db/id 17592186261824}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186260835} :answer-field/id #uuid "23816b2f-7629-5e86-9bf6-14c8e6ebed0d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262186}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=x\,i-5\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25.$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$

$$
r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.

"![](images/41/414611a90c2227ff163d40a4f6f560bc67c471fa0f35724e459cec280e4904f9.png)

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=4\,i+2\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\frac{t}{2}\,i+\frac{1}{2t}\,j$ for $t\in [\frac{1}{2},2],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](images/11/11376e6ef18b151a6dd1a02dd09f20b72bce3160c718f4095b4f08b23721ff1f.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\frac{t}{2},\,y=\frac{1}{2t}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =4, \\ Q(x,y) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t}{2})=\frac{1}{2}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2t})=-\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(4)\cdot (-\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}})-(2)\cdot (\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{2}{t}-t){|}_{1/2}^{2} \\  & =(1-2)-(4-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186262735 :question/id #uuid "1caebf8b-fbe2-5515-a0df-5bb50a3ced16" :question/math-academy-id "q-127227"} {:db/id 17592186262738 :question/id #uuid "d7df129a-7685-5a03-8c7b-340092011e9b" :question/math-academy-id "q-127233" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4b4f1bb5-5af8-54dc-b770-fd3f05a8066c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186260522} {:answer/id #uuid "5d592e34-b162-5fde-8afc-943efe3e8ed5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186260678} {:answer/id #uuid "ad49cef3-b98d-5033-a436-5ffab9049391" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186261392} {:answer/id #uuid "aeb8232e-688e-5fce-98f8-d1fc7d49d436" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186261415} {:answer/id #uuid "fdb10982-6a16-5384-8d48-742898dfa1f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186262100}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186260522} :answer-field/id #uuid "2c9c8acf-0dab-51c5-ade8-bb82d29c0b7f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262202}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "![](images/9b/9bb15934c271a17851342b9032f5096f48e7ac9ee4e149af92ac1010dea46d88.png)

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=3xy\,i+(2x+1)\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=t\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [0,1],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](images/0e/0e751adb9f44d24ba89af318fe5f063b1be146bbae45d05fc2dd9a99bef259f2.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =3xy=3{t}^{2}, \\ Q(x,y) & =2x+1=2t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3{t}^{2})(1)-(2t+1)(1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}-2t-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =({t}^{3}-{t}^{2}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1-1-1)-(0-0-0) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186262739 :question/id #uuid "b74be94c-a6f2-5d0a-8660-699d2ff2d45b" :question/math-academy-id "q-127244"} {:db/id 17592186262740 :question/id #uuid 17592186180725 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ be a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ and $C$ be a *closed* curve in the $xy$-plane. Recall that the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ is given by the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

Calculating flux using this definition is often cumbersome because we need to calculate $\mathbf n,$ the outward-pointing unit normal vector. 

In practice, we often use the following alternative formula to calculate the flux:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_C P\,\textrm{d}y- Q\,\textrm{d}x
$$

We'll derive this formula at the end of the lesson.

**Watch Out!** When applying this formula, we must choose a positively-oriented parameterization for $C.$ This formula will *not* work if $C$ is negatively oriented!" :tutorial/id #uuid "c74e835b-f210-5a77-8d6e-aef474c89522" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5851 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "cb889341-22d5-52e6-9979-1fd814bc5cec" :step/math-academy-id 35829 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180504}} {:db/id 17592186180507 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179746 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179608 :question/id #uuid "337d9d7e-5488-5e6d-af34-e01d22d3d0b9" :question/math-academy-id "e-9574"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "83a9ea5a-dcc8-51ed-90bc-dd684ef71ca9" :knowledge-point/question-generator {:db/id 17592186557574} :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180038} {:db/id 17592186180039} {:db/id 17592186262722} {:db/id 17592186262723} {:db/id 17592186262734} {:db/id 17592186262735} {:db/id 17592186262738} {:db/id 17592186262739} {:db/id 17592186262740} {:db/id 17592186262741} {:db/id 17592186362552} {:db/id 17592186421761} {:db/id 17592186421764}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Non-Closed Curve"} :step/id #uuid "f9195b98-bf60-5d80-a9f1-4dbe4c7ec614" :step/math-academy-id 35863 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180510}} {:db/id 17592186180509 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180727 :tutorial/content "As we've seen, the flux of a vector field $\mathbf F$ through a piecewise-smooth, closed curve $C$ is a unique scalar number that represents the net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ 

The question now is, does the notion of flux exist for curves that are not closed?

Indeed, it is possible to define the notion of flux through a non-closed curve. However, there is one crucial difference we need to bear in mind:

- In the case of a smooth, closed curve, it is always clear which direction is "out." Therefore, the outward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ is unique at every point on $C.$

- However, on a smooth, non-closed curve, there is no clear notion of "in" and "out." Instead, we can choose between *two* normal vectors at any point on the curve, as shown below.

![](images/d1/d193eb8109ead15de50c06a7bb0b654243173d882bd361f9fd34026aa23c1b5f.png)

Therefore, when computing the flux of a vector field through a non-closed curve, we first specify the direction that the unit normal points and then measure the flux relative to that direction. 

For example, for the vector field $\mathbf F$ and curve $C$ below, one choice for the unit normal will give a positive number, and the other a negative number.

![](images/4f/4f92dd5334b5836703857c081049f126d39c141e84d8e94171e338a162cf3cc4.png)

Finally, to calculate the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across a non-closed curve $C,$ we can continue to use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x.
$$

**Watch Out!** To apply this formula, we usually need to parameterize $C.$ It is *vital* that we pick a parameterization where the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ is a $90^\circ$ *clockwise* rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e2794e26-620d-59e9-85de-a3bb49f6991a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5869 :tutorial/title "Calculating Flux for Non-Closed Curves"} :step/id #uuid "c6cc7967-4281-527a-8021-7768a792728f" :step/math-academy-id 35901 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180507}} {:db/id 17592186180510 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180728 :tutorial/content "Let's now derive the following formula for the flux:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_C P\,\textrm{d}y- Q\,\textrm{d}x
$$

First, recall that if $C$ is parameterized by the function $\mathbf r(t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j$ for $t\in [a,b],$ then 

$$
\mathbf n = \dfrac{y'(t)\,\mathbf i - x'(t)\,\mathbf j}{||\mathbf r'(t)||},
$$

where it is assumed that $C$ is positively-oriented. 

Substituting our expression for $\mathbf n$ into our line integral definition of flux and using the fact that $\textrm d s = ||\mathbf r'(t)|| \,\textrm d t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{{y}^{′}(t)\,i-{x}^{′}(t)\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||})||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{{y}^{′}(t)\,i-{x}^{′}(t)\,j}{\cancel{||{r}^{′}(t)||}})\cancel{||{r}^{′}(t)||}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot ({y}^{′}(t)\,i-{x}^{′}(t)\,j)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}P(x(t),y(t)){y}^{′}(t)-Q(x(t),y(t)){x}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cc71a06d-4832-5949-91b4-71cb0f8185ca" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5870 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Main Formula"} :step/id #uuid "7543ee2e-ca36-5209-8a6f-1fae02154a3d" :step/math-academy-id 35902}] :activity/title "Calculating Flux in Two-Dimensional Vector Fields" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179867} {:db/id 17592186180506 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180725 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ be a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ and $C$ be a *closed* curve in the $xy$-plane. In practice, we often use the following alternative formula to calculate the flux:
