![](images/d1/d193eb8109ead15de50c06a7bb0b654243173d882bd361f9fd34026aa23c1b5f.png)

Therefore, when computing the flux of a vector field through a non-closed curve, we first specify the direction that the unit normal points and then measure the flux relative to that direction. 

For example, for the vector field $\mathbf F$ and curve $C$ below, one choice for the unit normal will give a positive number, and the other a negative number.

![](images/4f/4f92dd5334b5836703857c081049f126d39c141e84d8e94171e338a162cf3cc4.png)

Finally, to calculate the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across a non-closed curve $C,$ we can continue to use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x.
$$

**Watch Out!** To apply this formula, we usually need to parameterize $C.$ It is *vital* that we pick a parameterization where the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ is a $90^\circ$ *clockwise* rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e2794e26-620d-59e9-85de-a3bb49f6991a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5869 :tutorial/title "Calculating Flux for Non-Closed Curves"} {:db/id 17592186180728 :tutorial/content "Let's now derive the following formula for the flux:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_C P\,\textrm{d}y- Q\,\textrm{d}x
$$

First, recall that if $C$ is parameterized by the function $\mathbf r(t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j$ for $t\in [a,b],$ then 

$$
\mathbf n = \dfrac{y'(t)\,\mathbf i - x'(t)\,\mathbf j}{||\mathbf r'(t)||},
$$

where it is assumed that $C$ is positively-oriented. 

Substituting our expression for $\mathbf n$ into our line integral definition of flux and using the fact that $\textrm d s = ||\mathbf r'(t)|| \,\textrm d t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{{y}^{′}(t)\,i-{x}^{′}(t)\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||})||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{{y}^{′}(t)\,i-{x}^{′}(t)\,j}{\cancel{||{r}^{′}(t)||}})\cancel{||{r}^{′}(t)||}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot ({y}^{′}(t)\,i-{x}^{′}(t)\,j)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}P(x(t),y(t)){y}^{′}(t)-Q(x(t),y(t)){x}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cc71a06d-4832-5949-91b4-71cb0f8185ca" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5870 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Main Formula"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046660} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186547122} :activity/id #uuid "29222382-7ee7-520a-a03b-87b48ac36cf4" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050793 :topic/id #uuid "6768fffe-a644-5bd7-b35c-6b2cc2563786" :topic/math-academy-id 3716} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186547097 :step/content {:db/id 17592186262721 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6d6e8dc0-de0b-5246-baf1-2e88a94ead89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "25\pi " :db/id 17592186260835} {:answer/id #uuid "86aa0ca4-2fef-5ea7-ab52-7326ec1150e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-75\pi " :db/id 17592186261048} {:answer/id #uuid "945c2bc9-3eea-5671-ac58-7ea3e0a8ed17" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "150\pi " :db/id 17592186261168} {:answer/id #uuid "b7033798-e10d-5128-ab9b-7bc561366c39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-100\pi " :db/id 17592186261481} {:answer/id #uuid "dcaaf559-e7cf-5424-90bb-d31bc261f4d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "50\pi " :db/id 17592186261824}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186260835} :answer-field/id #uuid "23816b2f-7629-5e86-9bf6-14c8e6ebed0d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262186}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5660b13f-68bb-56f7-8d7c-83ccf48f3c64" :question/math-academy-id "q-127149" :question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=x\,i-5\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25.$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={5}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $5.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the double-angle formula for cosine, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-5)\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }25{cos}^{2}⁡t-25\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =25{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1}{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =25(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{4}+\frac{1}{2}t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =25(0+\pi +1)-(0+1) \\  & =25\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "244028d0-80f0-53fe-985b-068cd754088c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186547151}} {:db/id 17592186547122 :step/content {:db/id 17592186262715 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2e1109ed-b141-519b-a9c0-7e14a71dad93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "54" :db/id 17592186260290} {:answer/id #uuid "9c868b9a-1bd9-5569-9736-5eeff1693bf8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186261230} {:answer/id #uuid "d2368728-193a-54c0-a8d0-19ec801f6e17" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186261726} {:answer/id #uuid "d923b6e6-b8d4-5b4d-b3b3-1e5f1ccd3861" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186261792} {:answer/id #uuid "ff0167ac-6b4e-5d5c-aee1-3a42390d42e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "30" :db/id 17592186262111}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186261230} :answer-field/id #uuid "7e7bee21-7d21-5f74-b594-30d563e58eac" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262334}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "22f1827e-9056-5ca5-89c4-8b8f59040ce8" :question/math-academy-id "q-127142" :question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=7\,i+2\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=36.$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $6.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =7, \\ Q(x,y) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(7)\cdot (6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(2)\cdot (-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }42\operatorname{cos}⁡t+12\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(42\operatorname{sin}⁡t-12\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =(0-12)-(0-12) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8a5caabe-eb94-58e0-9030-d7df067be15b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186547176}} {:db/id 17592186547123 :step/content {:db/id 17592186262738 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4b4f1bb5-5af8-54dc-b770-fd3f05a8066c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186260522} {:answer/id #uuid "5d592e34-b162-5fde-8afc-943efe3e8ed5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186260678} {:answer/id #uuid "ad49cef3-b98d-5033-a436-5ffab9049391" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186261392} {:answer/id #uuid "aeb8232e-688e-5fce-98f8-d1fc7d49d436" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186261415} {:answer/id #uuid "fdb10982-6a16-5384-8d48-742898dfa1f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186262100}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186260522} :answer-field/id #uuid "2c9c8acf-0dab-51c5-ade8-bb82d29c0b7f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262202}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d7df129a-7685-5a03-8c7b-340092011e9b" :question/math-academy-id "q-127233" :question/problem "![](images/9b/9bb15934c271a17851342b9032f5096f48e7ac9ee4e149af92ac1010dea46d88.png)

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=3xy\,i+(2x+1)\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=t\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [0,1],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](images/0e/0e751adb9f44d24ba89af318fe5f063b1be146bbae45d05fc2dd9a99bef259f2.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =3xy=3{t}^{2}, \\ Q(x,y) & =2x+1=2t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3{t}^{2})(1)-(2t+1)(1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}-2t-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =({t}^{3}-{t}^{2}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1-1-1)-(0-0-0) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8ba5ec6f-d785-5185-aba1-3e57718869aa"} {:db/id 17592186547151 :step/content {:db/id 17592186262734 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2fd158a1-8e1c-5409-9f7d-cc713afefd91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{2}" :db/id 17592186260308} {:answer/id #uuid "49e0677d-703c-5fd2-bba6-5d10e8428357" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{9}{2}" :db/id 17592186260512} {:answer/id #uuid "afbd580d-7551-55b1-a2ab-a54c76c17535" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186261427} {:answer/id #uuid "d49ca082-e6c8-5be2-9a1d-8f3250a52777" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186261749} {:answer/id #uuid "f489697f-1e0a-5833-b73d-49cd2c52c047" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186262011}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186260512} :answer-field/id #uuid "fec87113-a1f7-5b61-8ed5-83eb792efa1a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262568}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d9d8ed81-5fd6-581e-8bd7-3dd3517c5bfe" :question/math-academy-id "q-127223" :question/problem "![](images/41/414611a90c2227ff163d40a4f6f560bc67c471fa0f35724e459cec280e4904f9.png)

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=4\,i+2\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\frac{t}{2}\,i+\frac{1}{2t}\,j$ for $t\in [\frac{1}{2},2],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](images/11/11376e6ef18b151a6dd1a02dd09f20b72bce3160c718f4095b4f08b23721ff1f.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\frac{t}{2},\,y=\frac{1}{2t}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =4, \\ Q(x,y) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t}{2})=\frac{1}{2}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2t})=-\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(4)\cdot (-\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}})-(2)\cdot (\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{2}{t}-t){|}_{1/2}^{2} \\  & =(1-2)-(4-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ca75fa0e-2e8e-54d5-8bf1-eb9a2e064862" :step/next {:db/id 17592186547123}} {:db/id 17592186547176 :step/content {:db/id 17592186262716 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a1393ce9-919a-5a3f-a8c5-3ce471d06ed6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186261276} {:answer/id #uuid "a40cd9e0-094a-53e2-bea7-72696c9a5f5c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186261304} {:answer/id #uuid "a5d88754-afb8-5215-960d-6c87c992d632" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186261315} {:answer/id #uuid "c6e3c02b-04d6-59c7-b162-6bd0c1725f86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186261634} {:answer/id #uuid "c73cd479-dfcc-5a7b-abdd-2aab64decf0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186261638}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186261638} :answer-field/id #uuid "f19e243a-d229-55b5-b933-2f21b1dc4b86" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262543}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "79c34a7b-b623-515b-8476-bf469364ea95" :question/math-academy-id "q-127143" :question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{3}\,i+{x}^{3}\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={1}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $1.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{3}={sin}^{3}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{3}={cos}^{3}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({cos}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t({sin}^{2}+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $6.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =7, \\ Q(x,y) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(7)\cdot (6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(2)\cdot (-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }42\operatorname{cos}⁡t+12\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(42\operatorname{sin}⁡t-12\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =(0-12)-(0-12) \\  & =0\end{aligned}

$$
r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the double-angle formula for cosine, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-5)\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }25{cos}^{2}⁡t-25\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =25{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1}{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =25(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{4}+\frac{1}{2}t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =25(0+\pi +1)-(0+1) \\  & =25\pi \end{aligned}

:question/math-academy-id "q-127223" :question/problem "![](images/41/414611a90c2227ff163d40a4f6f560bc67c471fa0f35724e459cec280e4904f9.png)

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=4\,i+2\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\frac{t}{2}\,i+\frac{1}{2t}\,j$ for $t\in [\frac{1}{2},2],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](images/11/11376e6ef18b151a6dd1a02dd09f20b72bce3160c718f4095b4f08b23721ff1f.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\frac{t}{2},\,y=\frac{1}{2t}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =4, \\ Q(x,y) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t}{2})=\frac{1}{2}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2t})=-\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(4)\cdot (-\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}})-(2)\cdot (\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{2}{t}-t){|}_{1/2}^{2} \\  & =(1-2)-(4-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ca75fa0e-2e8e-54d5-8bf1-eb9a2e064862" :step/next {:db/id 17592186547123}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2e1109ed-b141-519b-a9c0-7e14a71dad93" :answer/type {:db/id equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={1}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $1.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{3}={sin}^{3}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{3}={cos}^{3}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({cos}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t({sin}^{2}+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "fc626686-cd87-5458-bac3-97ad564bc475" :step/next {:db/id 17592186547097}} {:db/id 17592186547123 :step/content {:db/id 17592186262738 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4b4f1bb5-5af8-54dc-b770-fd3f05a8066c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186260522} {:answer/id #uuid "5d592e34-b162-5fde-8afc-943efe3e8ed5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186260678} {:answer/id #uuid "ad49cef3-b98d-5033-a436-5ffab9049391" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186261392} {:answer/id #uuid "aeb8232e-688e-5fce-98f8-d1fc7d49d436" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186261415} {:answer/id #uuid "fdb10982-6a16-5384-8d48-742898dfa1f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186262100}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186260522} :answer-field/id #uuid "2c9c8acf-0dab-51c5-ade8-bb82d29c0b7f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262202}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d7df129a-7685-5a03-8c7b-340092011e9b" :question/math-academy-id "q-127233" :question/problem "![](images/9b/9bb15934c271a17851342b9032f5096f48e7ac9ee4e149af92ac1010dea46d88.png)

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=3xy\,i+(2x+1)\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=t\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [0,1],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](images/0e/0e751adb9f44d24ba89af318fe5f063b1be146bbae45d05fc2dd9a99bef259f2.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =3xy=3{t}^{2}, \\ Q(x,y) & =2x+1=2t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3{t}^{2})(1)-(2t+1)(1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}-2t-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =({t}^{3}-{t}^{2}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1-1-1)-(0-0-0) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8ba5ec6f-d785-5185-aba1-3e57718869aa"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4b4f1bb5-5af8-54dc-b770-fd3f05a8066c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" "q-126717" :question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=y\,i-x\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-x=-5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }0\,\text{d}t \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1da0af94-7ee7-5f6d-819f-b12e5fd6862d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186552564}} {:db/id 17592186552555 :step/content {:db/id 17592186552504 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2d42fa31-693c-5e63-8b30-f714f163cf61" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16\pi " :db/id 17592186551774} {:answer/id #uuid "5a97f892-a6ec-5102-a2f8-b11ba307ea5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "64\pi " :db/id 17592186551880} {:answer/id #uuid "788d4fd5-7983-5bde-ac02-62cb31dfdb02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\pi " :db/id 17592186551948} {:answer/id #uuid "7bd545ee-d36f-5cc5-9368-52d6c0d580da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32\pi " :db/id 17592186551960} {:answer/id #uuid "ceda2cc6-35df-59c0-b345-80992bffb35d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186552157}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186551960} :answer-field/id #uuid "b1fc0cd0-57f3-5df9-9d82-31c607584763" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186552360}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "c696854b-d1cc-50f5-8398-3fba96da4739" :question/math-academy-id "q-127063" :question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=xi+\frac{1}{4}\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=8\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the double-angle formula for cosine, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (8\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(\frac{1}{4})\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }32{cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }32(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1}{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+16t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =(0+32\pi -1)-(0-1) \\  & =32\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3f3daaae-7b86-5566-920d-102af6de28ae" :step/next {:db/id 17592186552619}} {:db/id 17592186552564 :step/content {:db/id 17592186552492 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "52d243fe-78bb-52be-a2f0-f9815804e4d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186551859} {:answer/id #uuid "62fe97bc-579e-5ca3-9781-e68777e97322" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186551899} {:answer/id #uuid "86c104da-5667-58a2-96d7-fb45fe8f70c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186551990} {:answer/id #uuid "cc321452-9e74-5980-b3a3-7f6a5738db5e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186552153} {:answer/id #uuid "f2bc6932-c933-563c-a5c7-9780b5ef00c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6" :db/id 17592186552234}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186551859} :answer-field/id #uuid "0fe3669d-5fb8-5cf8-8402-eaff7b7d0308" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186552266}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b2316759-1f4d-59b3-aebb-24c5b1ac8267" :question/math-academy-id "q-127061" :question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{2}\,i-xy\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}=4{sin}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-xy=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt=du,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }6\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}6{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=49{cos}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,du=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(49{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(1)\cdot (-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98{cos}^{3}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-98{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{0}-98{u}^{2}\,du \\  & =(98\operatorname{sin}⁡t-7\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b7045b2d-6d96-5e8c-a2ed-01e6f608b548"} {:db/id 17592186552619 :step/content {:db/id 17592186552430 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d2b2827-fc94-5958-9a7b-16367fc19078" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8\pi " :db/id 17592186551698} {:answer/id #uuid "5bdc41c8-37d7-56e6-9cda-59976d63909e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4\pi " :db/id 17592186551887} {:answer/id #uuid "6c06907e-68fd-5846-846e-61d3ebbdcfb6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\pi " :db/id 17592186551915} {:answer/id #uuid "82ba78bb-4833-5028-9cf9-72e3cb59f32f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\pi " :db/id 17592186551975} {:answer/id #uuid "e9e5bb54-585e-59f5-8426-0a44c3083849" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186552213}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186552213} :answer-field/id #uuid "d2ae6c02-1c78-5b5d-926b-2d33957e08c9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186552374}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "4696ec15-27d3-55f9-a25e-60bb43e6e055" :question/math-academy-id "q-127075" :question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{3}\,i+(2+x)\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{3}=8{sin}^{3}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =2+x=2+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,du=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(8{sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(2+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t+16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{0}16{u}^{3}+16u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t{|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}=4{sin}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-xy=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }6\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}6{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=8\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the double-angle formula for cosine, as follows:

$$

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{3}=8{sin}^{3}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =2+x=2+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,du=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(8{sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(2+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t+16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{0}16{u}^{3}+16u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t{|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}

Calculate the length of the side $a$, giving your answer to the nearest tenth." :question/worked-solution "The Law of Cosines states that

$$
a^2 = b^2+c^2-2bc\cos{A}
$$

Here, we have

$$
m\angle A = 75^{\circ},\quad b = 10,\quad c=9
$$

Substituting the numbers into the formula gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
a^{2} &= 10^{2} + 9^{2} - 2(10)(9)\cos 75^{∘} \\
&= 100 + 81 - 180\cos 75^{∘} \\
&= 181 - 180 \cdot 0.2588… \\
&= 181 - 46.5874… \\
&= 134.4126
\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places

Taking the square root gives

$$

$$

\end{aligned}

The law of cosines is more general and can be used on *any* triangle.

**Note:** To remember the law of cosines, it's helpful to notice that the equations always follow the same pattern:

$$
(side opposite; the angle)^{2} = (adjacent; side)^{2} + (adjacent; other side)^{2} - 2(adjacent; side)(adjacent; other side)\cos (angle)

\end{aligned}

for any angle $A$ (this is the Pythagorean theorem in trigonometric form). Therefore, we have

$$
a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A
$$

as required.

$$

equations where the variable is in an exponent.
For instance, suppose we are given the equation 

$$
{\color{blue}2}^x=5.
$$

Notice that the base of the exponential is ${\color{blue}2}.$ So, if we take $\log_{\color{blue}2}$ of both sides of the equation, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡({2}^{x}) & ={log}_{2}⁡(5).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use the fact that $\log_{\color{blue}b} \left( {\color{blue}b}^c \right) = c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives

$$
x = \log_{\color{blue}2} (5).
$$

This is the solution! We often present the solution of an exponential equation as an exact solution in logarithmic form.

Note that when taking the $\log_b$ of both sides of an exponential equation, we always use the base of the exponential as the base of the logarithm." :tutorial/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "The standard equation of an upward- or downward-opening parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ is

$$
(x-h)^2 = 4p(y-k),
$$

where $p$ is a constant.

We can rewrite the given equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{2} & =4(2)(y-2).\end{aligned}
$$

It is now clear that our equation is of the standard type with $p =2.$

Comparing our equation with the standard equation, we can see that we have $h= -1$ and $k=2.$ Therefore, the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola are $(-1,2).$"} {:db/id 17592186048366} {:db/id $$
(y-k)^2 = 4p(x-h).
$$

The standard equation of an upward-opening or downward-opening parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ is

$$
(x-h)^2 = 4p(y-k).
$$

In either case, we can immediately retrieve the parabola's vertex if we're given an equation in either of these two forms.

**Note:** You might wonder why there is a $4$ in the $4p$ term. It turns out that the $4p$ term is necessary to represent a particular geometric property of the parabola, which we will learn about in the future. $$
(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),
$$

where $p$ is constant.

We can rewrite the given equation as 

$$
(y-0)^{2}=4(-\frac{2}{4})(x-1),
$$

which simplifies to

$$
(y-0)^{2}=4(-\frac{1}{2})(x-1).
$$

It is now clear that our equation is of the standard type with $p=-\frac{1}{2}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2} & >0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}>0}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivative of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}+{y}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ is defined only for 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2} & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} & ={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}>0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}>0}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186339041 :question/id #uuid "aa160777-02b6-5c38-ab2e-1a2020472567" :question/math-academy-id "q-72000" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124465 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8702032e-0795-5b51-9cc9-f89b35b64fa0" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Domain Where a Partial Derivative Exists"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "120d95db-561e-5ca1-ac7c-781d4f73d592" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z\ge 0}" :db/id 17592186336201} {:answer/id #uuid "57e0038e-1359-539c-a31a-4273eee9f3f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z=0}" :db/id 17592186336837} {:answer/id #uuid "bf81d1cd-2f00-5c28-8b65-d9f0805741aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z\le 0}" :db/id 17592186337733} {:answer/id #uuid "eeedecdd-29bc-53af-b9a1-39073c0ad4c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z\ne 0}" :db/id 17592186338122} {:answer/id #uuid "f21d2a1a-323a-5715-849a-37c24d5f3e67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z>0}" :db/id 17592186338151}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "f21d2a1a-323a-5715-849a-37c24d5f3e67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z>0}" :db/id 17592186338151} :answer-field/id #uuid "1bd98808-554a-5bf7-a091-d7cf355fddd2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186338328}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z),$ find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂z}$ exists." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)$ is defined only when

\begin{aligned}{f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)) \\  & =\frac{1}{x+y+z}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{z}(x,y,z)$ is defined only for 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $z$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z>0}\cap {(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z>0}.\end{aligned}

$$

So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y,z)\,:\,z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivative of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{x+y}\cdot \frac{1}{z} \\  & =\frac{1}{z(x+y)}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{z}(x,y,z)$ is defined only for 

$$
\begin{aligned}z(x+y) & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $z$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0}\cap {(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186382186 :question/id #uuid "085f5bf8-fd9d-5a03-95fc-bd2093188160" :question/math-academy-id "q-71999"} {:db/id 17592186382200 :question/id #uuid "4dd0e620-fdf6-56fb-b1ff-11292db39e41" :question/math-academy-id "q-72002"} {:db/id 17592186426721 :question/id #uuid "abe73768-66b7-589e-98db-9176084649e0" :question/math-academy-id "q-72006" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26545a18-833f-5099-8272-edbb2a66edaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186426703} {:answer/id #uuid "4d5bdc4f-f2f7-5295-b2ba-aa4588793c88" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,xy\ge 0\}" :db/id 17592186426706} {:answer/id #uuid "a9d10897-b8cf-5fad-b81e-91fbcac64c00" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{y}$ exists everywhere on the $xy$-plane" :db/id 17592186426710} {:answer/id #uuid "ebb0a6cd-e867-5b85-88ef-cd845e6904a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,xy<0\}" :db/id 17592186426714} {:answer/id #uuid "ff439fa7-e5eb-53d6-8dc0-e5396941eb06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}" :db/id 17592186426717}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426717} :answer-field/id #uuid "4cca11fe-f3bb-53ee-b7b6-de2725b37ad7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186426718}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy),$ find the set of values $(x,y)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ exists." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y)$ is defined when $xy>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is

17592186045487} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y})?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,1)$
- **II.** ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is defined
- **III.** ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that $f$ is defined only when

$$
\frac{x}{x+y}>0.
$$

At points in the domain of $f,$ we can compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{1\cdot (x+y)-x\cdot 1}{(x+y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{y}{(x+y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{y}{x(x+y)} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{x}{(x+y)^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. The function is defined at $(1,1),$ since

$$
f(1,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{1+1})=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}),
$$

and both partial derivatives are defined there:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =\frac{1}{1(1+1)}=\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =-\frac{1}{1+1}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. At $(0,1),$

$$
\frac{x}{x+y}=\frac{0}{0+1}=0,
$$

so

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0),
$$

which is undefined. Therefore, ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is not defined.

- Statement III is false for the same reason. Since $f$ is not defined at $(0,1),$ the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is not defined. The simplified expression $-\frac{1}{x+y}$ cannot be used to define the partial derivative at a point outside the domain of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186125000 :question/id #uuid "ff5209de-df39-5705-8c96-c53acb60628b" :question/math-academy-id "q-36522"} {:db/id 17592186268906 :question/id #uuid "72f1f14f-947a-5dd6-902d-418c94ea31fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-132675" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8e430633-0c79-5bd0-864a-cc54142526aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449496} {:answer/id #uuid "99da71ad-b733-50e9-9bc1-232efc6cef4b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449497}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449497} :answer-field/id #uuid "ad351a32-8420-5f40-bd4e-3a76a453aa9b" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450702} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3e1d2654-71e6-5045-abb7-876f75070a78" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449498} {:answer/id #uuid "9a1659ae-9585-5275-84c0-eb9540469367" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449499}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449498} :answer-field/id #uuid "f83c3b78-80d6-5799-ba6a-86046c4eb7a9" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450703} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b65c5da8-b876-59b5-b16a-4a0a833c5303" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449500} {:answer/id #uuid "c93dd213-5575-5cca-b228-64873eafdfe4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449501}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449500} :answer-field/id #uuid "db1f014c-1d1e-5df1-9579-1cb65d8ea1ac" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450704}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The partial derivative with respect to $y$ is defined at $(-1,-1,0)$
- **II.** ${f}_{x}(0,1,1)$ is defined
- **III.** ${f}_{z}(1,-1,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{z}{x} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{z}{y} \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(z) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(-1,-1,0)$, where we have 

$$
f(-1,-1,0)=0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡((-1)\cdot (-1))=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(-1,-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,-1,0) & =\frac{0}{(-1)}=0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(0,1,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,1,1)=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

- Statement III is also false. If we substitute $(1,-1,1)$ into ${f}_{z}$, we get

$$
{f}_{z}(1,-1,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot (-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1),
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."} {:db/id 17592186268907 :question/id #uuid "9dc50a8a-45d6-510c-8209-df3404b44621" :question/math-academy-id "q-132680" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9fc5f850-64cd-5893-8891-369f969391e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449502} {:answer/id #uuid "9c7c52c9-c826-5b11-9b7a-993392ba4ad3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449503}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449503} :answer-field/id #uuid "e0737846-2cd6-5da0-9650-75bc9876d5a8" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450705} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8b64dfe9-6cec-50a9-80d9-4a4526e80263" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449504} {:answer/id #uuid "6f04e2aa-8d8b-5312-ad91-326d2690aab0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449505}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449504} :answer-field/id #uuid "2de809ae-338b-5353-b9c7-b997f94a0161" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450706} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "edd0b63c-f4f5-5c2b-bd85-fa00f3b0bca4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449506} {:answer/id #uuid "6a6ab58d-d0b1-5f84-9b1f-39c31befd21b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449507}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449507} :answer-field/id #uuid "6f8beae8-a1f2-5630-bd94-336847d03d63" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450707}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{2}}?$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2x+y-z}?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(\sqrt{3},1)$
- **II.** ${f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})$ is defined
- **III.** ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(\sqrt{3},1)$, where we have 

$$
f(\sqrt{3},1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1})=\frac{\pi }{3},
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(\sqrt{3},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\sqrt{3},1) & =\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ {f}_{y}(\sqrt{3},1) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(1,\sqrt{3})$, where we have 

$$
f(1,\sqrt{3})=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=\frac{\pi }{6},
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,\sqrt{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is also true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{0}{1})=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(0,1)=-\frac{0}{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III"."} {:db/id 17592186409558 :question/id #uuid "538fdcf0-8dcd-525c-becd-0317742dbf1a" :question/math-academy-id "q-72010" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "899f43e4-fc9a-5506-b84d-a25c2d9eb6f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453928} {:answer/id #uuid "ec4690b4-12f7-5ffd-a0f0-d137fa95703c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453929}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453928} :answer-field/id #uuid "2ccf0ae7-dc64-51f0-892e-8d88c6910e82" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454714} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "376cf739-f8d8-5cb0-91a0-52b41ea250c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453930} {:answer/id #uuid "ffcc07c3-7704-591c-aebf-ff0249e9dd10" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453931}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453931} :answer-field/id #uuid "72f29120-e8c2-52fc-abd7-8386d5f878c4" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454715} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fc77c615-3280-58d4-a19d-18282a3f7486" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453932} {:answer/id #uuid "8cfc9ce4-4706-5c6b-8f71-059b43d404d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453933}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453932} :answer-field/id #uuid "a7c89136-ff34-5898-9f58-5a98f17bcfb1" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454716}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,-1)$

- **II.** ${f}_{y}(-1,-1)$ is defined

- **III.** ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}\cdot \frac{y}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\  & =\frac{y{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}\cdot \frac{x}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\  & =\frac{x{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2\sqrt{xy}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one. 

- Statement I is false. If we substitute $(1,-1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)}}=-{e}^{\sqrt{-1}}
$$

which is undefined since we have a negative number under the radical.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(-1,-1)$, where we have 

$$
f(-1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{1}}={e}^{1}=e,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,-1) & =\frac{(-1){e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}}{2\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}=-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1}}}{2\sqrt{1}}=-\frac{e}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(0,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,1)=1\cdot \frac{{e}^{\sqrt{0\cdot 1}}}{2\sqrt{0\cdot 1}}=\frac{{e}^{0}}{2\sqrt{0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II  only'."} {:db/id 17592186436752 :question/id #uuid "efd3e6cc-b29d-5cd4-ba97-6a3820c7c7c6" :question/math-academy-id "q-132672"} {:db/id 17592186493937 :question/id #uuid "970e7795-a408-5210-80aa-25f375509b0b" :question/math-academy-id "q-65263" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "084ca7fb-683b-515d-bd79-6b47f18630b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186493404} {:answer/id #uuid "1352f5a0-9197-5682-a147-c4c731774502" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186493425} {:answer/id #uuid "6a0ef88e-c7ac-5cdc-ae0e-1efc196b01b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186493549} {:answer/id #uuid "82a72c3b-2c62-5d09-a02a-39b20b9aa673" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186493599} {:answer/id #uuid "d3bc4946-5ae0-59ab-8397-c509f69337df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186493726}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493549} :answer-field/id #uuid "8c27c81b-25fa-5185-a05b-37e0f78454cf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493847}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}?$

II. ${f}_{y}(-1,1,1)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{z}(1,1,0)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-1,-1) & =\frac{(-1)(-1){e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}}{2\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1}}}{2\sqrt{1}}=\frac{e}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(-1,1,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(-1,1,1)={e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(1)(1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{-1}},
$$

which is undefined since we have a negative number under the radical. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

$$
{f}_{z}(1,1,0)=\frac{1\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}}{2\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

:question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xyz)$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{yz}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{xz}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{xy}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xyz)$ is defined only when $-1\le xyz\le 1.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le xyz\le 1\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{yz}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}}$ is defined only when 

$$
\begin{aligned}1-(xyz)^{2} & >0 \\ (xyz)^{2} & <1 \\ |xyz| & <1,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives $-1<xyz<1.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le xyz\le 1\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186125193 :question/id #uuid "0790aa49-4020-5e37-b9fd-2a18a4aa638d" :question/math-academy-id "q-65252" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124557 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e2d7d4db-e9e1-54a0-aadb-42447771855d" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Domain Where All Partial Derivatives Exist"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "28861c2c-ac02-5058-a869-4e0465790ba2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,y>0}" :db/id 17592186333364} {:answer/id #uuid "667aa589-f213-58d8-80cb-0bd6003e45d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,xy\ge 0}" :db/id 17592186333924} {:answer/id #uuid "b2322b57-77ca-5063-9b19-1f81d4ecf5f6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0}" :db/id 17592186334552} {:answer/id #uuid "b6f16518-f4d1-5447-8c6d-28607b0b21e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,xy<0}" :db/id 17592186334591} {:answer/id #uuid "d8b23563-bef9-5ca0-84f5-e8348fe229b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0}" :db/id 17592186334888}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "b2322b57-77ca-5063-9b19-1f81d4ecf5f6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0}" :db/id 17592186334552} :answer-field/id #uuid "4339d5d0-363f-5656-970d-cbfe0eaaac6f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186335365}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{y},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y)$ where all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$ is defined only when $xy>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y)\,:\,xy>0}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y)=1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$ is defined only when $xy>0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}={(x,y)\,:\,xy>0}.
$$

- The function ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & ={(x,y)\,:\,xy>0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,xy>0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y)\,:\,xy>0}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186268902 :question/id #uuid "a66c3ca8-3dc1-5636-a0ae-fd45747b8bcc" :question/math-academy-id "q-132649"} {:db/id 17592186268903 :question/id #uuid "f03ff15b-864a-54f0-95c4-85eaad4622ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-132650" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1e9af209-8790-5051-b760-8a2b7ab58c1e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1\}" :db/id 17592186493443} {:answer/id #uuid "2ae2e06a-4a60-5d0a-89f7-a1206ad8886c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186493462} {:answer/id #uuid "4da31340-f280-5ea2-b625-950af86420b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1\}" :db/id 17592186493517} {:answer/id #uuid "ee12a67f-64f9-5a94-956a-3d8cefbc2906" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0,\,z>0\}" :db/id 17592186493770} {:answer/id #uuid "f1099e4d-5739-5e2b-abdc-97a47dbd0d32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186493778}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493462} :answer-field/id #uuid "544bcd11-f607-53b0-99d1-1273ed387e89" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268559}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given that $g(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{z}$ and

$$
\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{2y}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)},\,\frac{∂g}{∂z}=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{{z}^{2}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $g$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $g(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{z}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is 

$$
{D}_{g}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${g}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{2x}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1\ne 0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domain of ${g}_{y}(x,y,z)$ is the same: 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{y}}={D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function ${g}_{z}(x,y,z)=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{{z}^{2}}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{z}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{z}} & ={D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{z}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & \,\,\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & \,\,\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}\end{aligned}

find the set of values $(x,y)$ where all partial derivatives of $g$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is 

$$
{D}_{g}=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${g}_{x}(x,y)=\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0\}.
$$

- The function ${g}_{y}(x,y)=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{y}}=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{y}} & =\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0\}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186339044 :question/id #uuid "af4cc0a9-980f-5d30-aeb4-1f5c6677cbac" :question/math-academy-id "q-72008"} {:db/id 17592186339046 :question/id #uuid "a87fd165-97e3-5aaa-8695-7d41aa3480e0" :question/math-academy-id "q-72025"} {:db/id 17592186339047 :question/id #uuid "b7c74b46-8f2a-5a21-a1ce-e71252b0fbf4" :question/math-academy-id "q-72027"} {:db/id 17592186381048 :question/id #uuid "cb51f4b0-9af5-582f-b38f-08847728e4c9" :question/math-academy-id "q-132655"} {:db/id 17592186382207 :question/id #uuid "07b7a4d5-0d88-5759-b677-08d7e8ac3fca" :question/math-academy-id "q-72007" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "32e88f5b-98b5-56cf-80ff-82851c3303b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ge 0,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186445248} {:answer/id #uuid "395e6ad4-f871-5195-aed0-c82a5612a79c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z>0\}" :db/id 17592186445249} {:answer/id #uuid "410d16c0-a17f-5bb6-8557-36dd6a7c08d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ne 0,z<0\}" :db/id 17592186445250} {:answer/id #uuid "629c6583-5abe-5cd2-8098-b6cded7ee4e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186445252} {:answer/id #uuid "a318ea21-95fd-5a51-9e1e-c2501bcf0d2e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy=0,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186445254}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186445252} :answer-field/id #uuid "bb805034-5a71-5881-8d6e-dc2faac4f6f6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186382208}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{z}$ and

$$
