$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{z}$ is defined only when $xy\ge 0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ge 0,z\ne 0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}=\frac{y{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2z\sqrt{xy}}$ is defined only when $xy>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domain of ${f}_{y}=\frac{x{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2z\sqrt{xy}}$ is the same

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function ${f}_{z}=-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{{z}^{2}}$ is defined only when $xy\ge 0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ge 0,z\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ge 0,z\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0\}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186409559 :question/id #uuid "5744243e-c58b-5537-916f-bee0cb473253" :question/math-academy-id "q-132654" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1625c29f-0f6c-51a9-9abf-da854c690be8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0,\,x+y+z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186445247} {:answer/id #uuid "603bfd17-5e73-595d-9e4e-67eb66547b83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}" :db/id 17592186445251} {:answer/id #uuid "6e5cf9f7-9ed5-55ea-b3dd-342a00251b3b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0,\,y\ne 0,\,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186445253} {:answer/id #uuid "b33e9175-1fe3-525c-84d8-993f2fb37971" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z>0\}" :db/id 17592186445255} {:answer/id #uuid "d2f2980b-11d7-556d-9928-b285bb77ebda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz\ge 0\}" :db/id 17592186445256}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186445251} :answer-field/id #uuid "c3c16b06-37a6-5eac-b3ba-318617c8302e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186409555}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{z},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$ is defined only when $xyz>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x}$ is defined only when $x\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{y}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{z}$ is defined only when $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186426720 :question/id #uuid "13585dd1-9ab5-5887-870c-2d899c40d4a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-132652" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9a414987-4111-5550-9b84-35b48e518248" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0,\,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z" :db/id 17592186426709} {:answer/id #uuid "c4574d37-c2e2-5922-8956-3143f5bef26f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y>0,\,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186426712} {:answer/id #uuid "c67ec9fa-9f76-59b9-b6ed-a85557705824" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y>0,\,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z" :db/id 17592186426713} {:answer/id #uuid "ee7e5c9b-05ac-5232-9af8-bc55f1d66335" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,\,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186426715} {:answer/id #uuid "f480f4b0-b440-57d3-be41-894b18986911" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,\,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z" :db/id 17592186426716}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426716} :answer-field/id #uuid "4d0f4a07-8c58-5c53-b0aa-71dedf0ab601" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186426719}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ and

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186436749 :question/id #uuid "9a747118-95ab-56ac-85bf-8bf99184999c" :question/math-academy-id "q-132660"} {:db/id 17592186436751 :question/id #uuid defined *and* the partial derivative is defined.

For example, let's consider the function $f(x,y) = \ln(xy).$ We wish to determine the set of values $(x,y)$ on which the partial derivative $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ exists.

First, we need to find the domain of $f$ since we cannot differentiate $f$ at any point that lies outside of its domain. The natural logarithm is defined only for positive inputs, so the domain of $f$ is 

$$
D_f = \{ (x,y)\, : \, xy > 0 \}.
$$

Next, we compute the partial derivative:

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \dfrac{1}{x}
$$

The partial derivative $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ (also denoted $f_x$) is not defined at $x=0.$ So, the domain of $f_x$ is

$$
D_{f_x} = \{ (x,y)\, : \, x \ne 0 \}.
$$

To compute the set where  $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ exists, we take the intersection of the domain of the original function $(D_f)$ with the domain of the partial derivative $(D_{f_x})$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,x\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ exists on the set $\{ (x,y)\, : \, xy \gt 0 \}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5862db65-6f2d-5256-968d-cb971dd6b2f1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2532 #uuid "f4cc9d43-0b3e-5cd2-8e04-c1f0f43e9e2a" :step/math-academy-id 11429 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125314}} {:db/id 17592186125314 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125742 :tutorial/content "From single-variable calculus, if a function $y=f(x)$ is differentiable at a point, then it is continuous at that point.

But for a multivariable function, even if all partial derivatives are defined at a certain point, it **does not mean** that the function is continuous at that point!

The reason why partial differentiability does not imply continuity in the case of a multivariable function is that

- the existence of the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ depend only on the behavior of $f$ parallel to the $x$- and $y$-axes, whereas

- the continuity of $f$ depends on its behavior as we approach $(x_0,y_0)$ from any direction.

For example, let's consider the following multivariable function:

![](images/cb/cb5aad599789d1e317ff3ddc07eaa418e80469307f67e98e2108660fc7d15701.svg)

The function $f$ is defined at the point $(0,0)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f(0,0)=0
$$

Likewise, the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ are both defined at the point $(0,0).$ We can compute them using the limit definition of the partial derivative, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,0) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[f(0+h,0)-f(0,0)] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[\frac{(h)(0)}{{h}^{2}+{0}^{2}}-0] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[0-0] \\  & =0 \\ {f}_{y}(0,0) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[f(0,0+h)-f(0,0)] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[\frac{(0)(h)}{{0}^{2}+{h}^{2}}-0] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[0-0] \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So the partial derivatives both exist at $(0,0).$ We will now show that the function is not continuous at $(0,0).$

For the function $f$ to be continuous at $(0,0),$ the limit of the function must be equal to the function value, regardless of the path taken. So, we must have

$$
\lim\limits_{(x,y) \to (0,0)}  f(x,y) = f(0,0) =0.
$$

However, this is not the case here. When we evaluate the limit along the path $y=x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{(x,y)\to (0,0)\,\,y=x}f(x,y) & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{x\cdot x}{{x}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2} \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our function $f(x,y)$ is *not* continuous at the point $(0,0),$ even though both of its partial derivatives exist there." :tutorial/id #uuid "ca47070b-a1d3-53ad-8f57-2dbd4e770dce" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2533 :tutorial/title "Partial Differentiability Does Not Imply Continuity"} :step/id #uuid "f23e88d8-c204-5795-b172-b05000a202c3" :step/math-academy-id 11432} {:db/id 17592186125463 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124557 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124366 :question/id #uuid "97192aac-6c1a-5ead-962b-0bf7ab573661" :question/math-academy-id "e-6109"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e2d7d4db-e9e1-54a0-aadb-42447771855d" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125001} {:db/id 17592186125193} {:db/id 17592186268902} {:db/id 17592186268903} {:db/id 17592186268904} {:db/id 17592186339043} {:db/id 17592186339044} {:db/id 17592186339046} {:db/id 17592186339047} {:db/id 17592186381048} {:db/id 17592186382207} {:db/id 17592186409559} {:db/id 17592186426720} {:db/id 17592186436749} {:db/id 17592186436751} {:db/id 17592186559825}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Domain Where All Partial Derivatives Exist"} :step/id #uuid "c86dfe84-cedf-55cf-bf44-efb12a49ac66" :step/math-academy-id 22675 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125313}}] :activity/title "Partial Differentiability of Multivariable Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124725} {:db/id 17592186125311 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125741 :tutorial/content "The partial derivative of a function exists where the original function is defined *and* the partial derivative is defined.

\begin{aligned}{lim}_{(x,y)\to (0,0)\,\,y=x}f(x,y) & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{x\cdot x}{{x}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2} \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our function $f(x,y)$ is *not* continuous at the point $(0,0),$ even though both of its partial derivatives exist there." :tutorial/id #uuid "ca47070b-a1d3-53ad-8f57-2dbd4e770dce" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2533 :tutorial/title "Partial Differentiability Does Not Imply Continuity"} :step/id #uuid "f23e88d8-c204-5795-b172-b05000a202c3" :step/math-academy-id 11432} {:db/id 17592186125742 :tutorial/content "From single-variable calculus, if a function $y=f(x)$ is differentiable at a point, then it is continuous at that point.

But for a multivariable function, even if all partial derivatives are defined at a certain point, it **does not mean** that the function is continuous at that point!

The reason why partial differentiability does not imply continuity in the case of a multivariable function is that

- the existence of the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ depend only on the behavior of $f$ parallel to the $x$- and $y$-axes, whereas

- the continuity of $f$ depends on its behavior as we approach $(x_0,y_0)$ from any direction.

For example, let's consider the following multivariable function:

![](images/cb/cb5aad599789d1e317ff3ddc07eaa418e80469307f67e98e2108660fc7d15701.svg)

The function $f$ is defined at the point $(0,0)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f(0,0)=0
$$

Likewise, the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ are both defined at the point $(0,0).$ We can compute them using the limit definition of the partial derivative, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,0) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[f(0+h,0)-f(0,0)] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[\frac{(h)(0)}{{h}^{2}+{0}^{2}}-0] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[0-0] \\  & =0 \\ {f}_{y}(0,0) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[f(0,0+h)-f(0,0)] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[\frac{(0)(h)}{{0}^{2}+{h}^{2}}-0] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[0-0] \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So the partial derivatives both exist at $(0,0).$ We will now show that the function is not continuous at $(0,0).$

For the function $f$ to be continuous at $(0,0),$ the limit of the function must be equal to the function value, regardless of the path taken. So, we must have

$$
\lim\limits_{(x,y) \to (0,0)}  f(x,y) = f(0,0) =0.
$$

However, this is not the case here. When we evaluate the limit along the path $y=x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{(x,y)\to (0,0)\,\,y=x}f(x,y) & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{x\cdot x}{{x}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2} \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our function $f(x,y)$ is *not* continuous at the point $(0,0),$ even though both of its partial derivatives exist there." :tutorial/id #uuid "ca47070b-a1d3-53ad-8f57-2dbd4e770dce" "q-72010" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,-1)$

- **II.** ${f}_{y}(-1,-1)$ is defined

- **III.** ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}\cdot \frac{y}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\  & =\frac{y{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}\cdot \frac{x}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\  & =\frac{x{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2\sqrt{xy}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one. 

- Statement I is false. If we substitute $(1,-1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)}}=-{e}^{\sqrt{-1}}
$$

which is undefined since we have a negative number under the radical.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(-1,-1)$, where we have 

$$
f(-1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{1}}={e}^{1}=e,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,-1) & =\frac{(-1){e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}}{2\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}=-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1}}}{2\sqrt{1}}=-\frac{e}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(0,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,1)=1\cdot \frac{{e}^{\sqrt{0\cdot 1}}}{2\sqrt{0\cdot 1}}=\frac{{e}^{0}}{2\sqrt{0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II  only'."} :step/id #uuid "06a4b700-aa67-595f-ad77-c3a9c2d08fa3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186409563}} {:db/id 17592186409561 :step/content {:db/id 17592186339043 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00e7e3fe-8aa5-5dbe-b351-f8ab041da26a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186559016} {:answer/id #uuid "3d4cb978-08f2-56c9-a2ea-886a3b926325" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0\}" :db/id 17592186559174} {:answer/id #uuid "6e834be1-c403-5b49-87e3-229d8e48f719" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=0\}" :db/id 17592186559289} {:answer/id #uuid "783fd4c1-fb89-5517-bc35-b883098e9f40" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<0\}" :db/id 17592186559318} {:answer/id #uuid "e4c394bb-40ee-5d34-8bd0-d21a98e21ea0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ge 0\}" :db/id 17592186559581}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186559174} :answer-field/id #uuid "167ce942-9903-5739-b46e-634adbd1db2c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338315}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "329fb25a-c39e-587a-8c51-720f867dc9e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-72005" :question/problem "Given that $g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ and

$$
\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}),\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y)$ where all partial derivatives of $g$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is 

$$
{D}_{g}=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${g}_{x}(x,y)=\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0\}.
$$

- The function ${g}_{y}(x,y)=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{y}}=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{y}} & =\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0\}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1786d23c-6b2b-5b25-8a34-a3df54af58bf" :step/next {:db/id 17592186409560}} {:db/id 17592186409562 :step/content {:db/id 17592186335822 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "39c4f7c1-2cc1-57ed-a18b-bf91992e00d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186451483} {:answer/id #uuid "f3e4c2de-8568-5ff2-baf8-40d15c25b5ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186451484}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186451484} :answer-field/id #uuid "99c60c75-d597-5852-8b29-5420ba46e80b" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186452589} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "96e8d67b-c006-521e-ad4e-1b3b5e5bbae0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186451485} {:answer/id #uuid "5fcff0a4-c6d8-5ff7-9344-ecba3634e8b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186451486}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186451485} :answer-field/id #uuid "bf8a887b-1bb0-5b36-af98-54f46b4ff833" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186452590} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1bd09d87-8f09-5958-88e2-49043d0205b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186451487} {:answer/id #uuid "72089ef2-d948-531c-b1f3-ac84e9dc1b0d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186451488}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186451488} :answer-field/id #uuid "6d4fe7e1-7135-5cca-a3a0-20d39be1b879" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186452591}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b22bd39f-49d5-56c7-8797-705e83876e55" :question/math-academy-id "q-65255" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=xy{e}^{x/y}?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${f}_{x}(0,1)$is defined

- **II.** ${f}_{y}(1,0)$ is defined

- **III.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,1)$" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{e}^{x/y}) \\  & =y{e}^{x/y}+xy{e}^{x/y}(\frac{1}{y}) \\  & =y{e}^{x/y}+x{e}^{x/y} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{e}^{x/y}) \\  & =x{e}^{x/y}+xy{e}^{x/y}(-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =x{e}^{x/y}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}{e}^{x/y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,1)=0\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{0/1}=0,
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1)=1\cdot {e}^{0/1}+0\cdot {e}^{0/1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,0)$ into ${f}_{y}$, we get

$$
{f}_{y}(1,0)=1\cdot {e}^{1/0}-\frac{{1}^{2}}{0}\cdot {e}^{1/0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,1)=1\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{1/1}=e,
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =1\cdot {e}^{1/1}+1\cdot {e}^{1/1}=2e \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =1\cdot {e}^{1/1}-\frac{{1}^{2}}{1}\cdot {e}^{1/1}=e-e=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only"."} :step/id #uuid "488b6ab6-cae5-5979-9b52-c3723c3f093b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186409561}} {:db/id 17592186409563 :step/content {:db/id 17592186409559 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1625c29f-0f6c-51a9-9abf-da854c690be8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0,\,x+y+z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186445247} {:answer/id #uuid "603bfd17-5e73-595d-9e4e-67eb66547b83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}" :db/id 17592186445251} {:answer/id #uuid "6e5cf9f7-9ed5-55ea-b3dd-342a00251b3b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0,\,y\ne 0,\,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186445253} {:answer/id #uuid "b33e9175-1fe3-525c-84d8-993f2fb37971" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z>0\}" :db/id 17592186445255} {:answer/id #uuid "d2f2980b-11d7-556d-9928-b285bb77ebda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz\ge 0\}" :db/id 17592186445256}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186445251} :answer-field/id #uuid "c3c16b06-37a6-5eac-b3ba-318617c8302e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186409555}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5744243e-c58b-5537-916f-bee0cb473253" :question/math-academy-id "q-132654" :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{z},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$ is defined only when $xyz>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x}$ is defined only when $x\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{y}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{z}$ is defined only when $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "61817e36-5704-54ae-b054-a7bf550b56c7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186409564}} {:db/id 17592186409564 :step/content {:db/id 17592186409557 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e148fac7-727b-55d9-ba67-0a9fc7a276e4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453368} {:answer/id #uuid "6c6ec723-5cd2-5173-b8f1-1778f583295d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453369}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453369} :answer-field/id #uuid "4e8e1392-18d1-56b3-b0f5-ff3dd861687a" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454434} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a536093-cb71-5d44-a52f-8e05b4b9f74a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453370} {:answer/id #uuid "cc2d5ab2-a228-5241-aef5-decbffea282c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453371}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453371} :answer-field/id #uuid "deacc4af-75f1-5a94-a0d0-5d1ad4ac3ea8" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454435} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "80b4f556-0cc0-5fc7-9fac-56ff9260d6c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453372} {:answer/id #uuid "cbd91732-9818-5742-9c5d-ea668d6dbe0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453373}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453373} :answer-field/id #uuid "7f7af479-38a3-58de-bca6-c137a88e2790" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454436}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0a3b6388-98bd-5083-8d1c-f60a05890b23" :question/math-academy-id "q-132726" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(\sqrt{3},1)$
- **II.** ${f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})$ is defined
- **III.** ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(\sqrt{3},1)$, where we have 

$$
f(\sqrt{3},1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1})=\frac{\pi }{3},
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(\sqrt{3},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\sqrt{3},1) & =\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ {f}_{y}(\sqrt{3},1) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(1,\sqrt{3})$, where we have 

$$

- **II.** ${f}_{y}(1,0)$ is defined

- **III.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,1)$" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{e}^{x/y}) \\  & =y{e}^{x/y}+xy{e}^{x/y}(\frac{1}{y}) \\  & =y{e}^{x/y}+x{e}^{x/y} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{e}^{x/y}) \\  & =x{e}^{x/y}+xy{e}^{x/y}(-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =x{e}^{x/y}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}{e}^{x/y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,1)=0\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{0/1}=0,
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1)=1\cdot {e}^{0/1}+0\cdot {e}^{0/1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,0)$ into ${f}_{y}$, we get

$$
{f}_{y}(1,0)=1\cdot {e}^{1/0}-\frac{{1}^{2}}{0}\cdot {e}^{1/0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,1)=1\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{1/1}=e,
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =1\cdot {e}^{1/1}+1\cdot {e}^{1/1}=2e \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =1\cdot {e}^{1/1}-\frac{{1}^{2}}{1}\cdot {e}^{1/1}=e-e=0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

"q-132654" :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{z},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$ is defined only when $xyz>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x}$ is defined only when $x\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{y}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{z}$ is defined only when $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "61817e36-5704-54ae-b054-a7bf550b56c7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186409564}} {:db/id 17592186409561 :step/content {:db/id 17592186339043 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00e7e3fe-8aa5-5dbe-b351-f8ab041da26a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186559016} {:answer/id #uuid "3d4cb978-08f2-56c9-a2ea-886a3b926325" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0\}" :db/id 17592186559174} {:answer/id #uuid "6e834be1-c403-5b49-87e3-229d8e48f719" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=0\}" :db/id 17592186559289} {:answer/id #uuid "783fd4c1-fb89-5517-bc35-b883098e9f40" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<0\}" :db/id 17592186559318} {:answer/id #uuid "e4c394bb-40ee-5d34-8bd0-d21a98e21ea0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ge 0\}" :db/id 17592186559581}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186559174} :answer-field/id #uuid "167ce942-9903-5739-b46e-634adbd1db2c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338315}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "329fb25a-c39e-587a-8c51-720f867dc9e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-72005" :question/problem "Given that $g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ and

$$

$f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(\sqrt{3},1)$
- **II.** ${f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})$ is defined
- **III.** ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(\sqrt{3},1)$, where we have 

$$
f(\sqrt{3},1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1})=\frac{\pi }{3},
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(\sqrt{3},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\sqrt{3},1) & =\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ {f}_{y}(\sqrt{3},1) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(1,\sqrt{3})$, where we have 

$$
f(1,\sqrt{3})=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=\frac{\pi }{6},
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,\sqrt{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is also true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{0}{1})=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(0,1)=-\frac{0}{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III"."} :step/id #uuid "be87cbb6-8a21-5895-a193-08d9d1a311c5"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e148fac7-727b-55d9-ba67-0a9fc7a276e4" "q-72022" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy(z-1))?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The partial derivative with respect to $z$ is defined at $(3,2,1)$

- **II.** ${f}_{y}(1,1,2)$ is defined

- **III.** ${f}_{x}(1,2,3)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot y(z-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot x(z-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot xy \\  & =\frac{1}{z-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.  

- Statement I is false. If we substitute $(3,2,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(3,2,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot 2\cdot (1-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0),
$$

which is undefined.

- Statement II is true. If we substitute $(1,1,2)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,1,2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot (2-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,1,2) & =\frac{1}{1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. If we substitute $(1,2,3)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,2,3)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 2\cdot (3-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4),
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,2,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,2,3) & =\frac{1}{1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III  only'."} :step/id #uuid "30fe1f41-c7f8-5010-a260-ed3ef63a4abc" :step/next {:db/id 17592186426726}} {:db/id 17592186426723 :step/content {:db/id 17592186268914 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "be072909-07f4-5637-903f-a70436d30a22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449508} {:answer/id #uuid "049c935c-a4ee-5a02-b019-9fd190c4913a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449509}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449509} :answer-field/id #uuid "548fb633-f107-5482-81d5-3893faff9da9" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450708} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6299e699-f9eb-5bb0-bad6-16b58253ff62" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449510} {:answer/id #uuid "1a54ebb4-bb0e-5d8c-89d3-811768de2241" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449511}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449510} :answer-field/id #uuid "d8cc1d60-0069-586b-b1d2-3edcc2ab8a3a" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450709} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c3e18ad-85a1-5207-a031-4d811fa7f0dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449512} {:answer/id #uuid "b0e9a6dd-aa8d-53df-aa34-38929292da67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449513}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449512} :answer-field/id #uuid "abb845e0-0f31-593e-85f2-f6c94ef89a74" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450710}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a68d3690-fbcf-53d1-acbf-a5134efed5cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-132728" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2)?$

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(0,2)$

- **II.** ${f}_{x}(1,0)$ is defined

- **III.** ${f}_{y}(1,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(0,2)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡2,
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,2) & =\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=0 \\ {f}_{y}(0,2) & =\frac{2(2)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,0)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{0}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1)
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is also false. If we substitute $(1,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{1}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0)
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

$$

$$

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le xyz\le 1\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.\end{aligned}

$$

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$

$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "dd470b32-cbc1-54d2-9ca1-54631aa728a9" :step/next {:db/id 17592186426723}}] :activity/title "Partial Differentiability of Multivariable Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186426702} {:db/id 17592186426724 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125001 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "323e1e26-806d-5103-9c5b-05be999f86f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}" :db/id 17592186426704} {:answer/id #uuid "3f71ffa0-c375-5e54-a4b4-82c47e1862fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0<xyz<1\}" :db/id 17592186426705} {:answer/id #uuid "58a495bb-1535-5c0c-8153-9cddc1a1d72c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz\ge 0\}" :db/id 17592186426707} {:answer/id #uuid "66b51739-6d9c-59ee-81d0-4f21e588a03b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le xyz\le 1\}" :db/id 17592186426708} {:answer/id #uuid "ab77e5e6-52f4-5889-9394-0781e3a0ecd5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}" :db/id 17592186426711}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426704} :answer-field/id #uuid "6476017e-359c-522d-8dec-b6d7cd0832c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186122606}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f23029a5-0003-5b31-a62a-a58e0c29de2f" :question/math-academy-id "q-36527" :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xyz)$ and

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The partial derivative with respect to $z$ is defined at $(3,2,1)$

- **II.** ${f}_{y}(1,1,2)$ is defined

- **III.** ${f}_{x}(1,2,3)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot y(z-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot x(z-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot xy \\  & =\frac{1}{z-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.  

- Statement I is false. If we substitute $(3,2,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(3,2,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot 2\cdot (1-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0),
$$

which is undefined.

- Statement II is true. If we substitute $(1,1,2)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,1,2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot (2-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,1,2) & =\frac{1}{1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. If we substitute $(1,2,3)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,2,3)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 2\cdot (3-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4),
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,2,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,2,3) & =\frac{1}{1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III  only'."} :step/id #uuid "30fe1f41-c7f8-5010-a260-ed3ef63a4abc" :step/next {:db/id 17592186426726}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid \frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{y{sin}^{2}⁡z}
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "dd470b32-cbc1-54d2-9ca1-54631aa728a9" :step/next {:db/id 17592186426723}} {:db/id 17592186426723 :step/content {:db/id 17592186268914 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "be072909-07f4-5637-903f-a70436d30a22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449508} {:answer/id #uuid "049c935c-a4ee-5a02-b019-9fd190c4913a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449509}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449509} :answer-field/id #uuid "548fb633-f107-5482-81d5-3893faff9da9" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450708} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6299e699-f9eb-5bb0-bad6-16b58253ff62" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449510} {:answer/id #uuid "1a54ebb4-bb0e-5d8c-89d3-811768de2241" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449511}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449510} :answer-field/id #uuid "d8cc1d60-0069-586b-b1d2-3edcc2ab8a3a" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450709} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c3e18ad-85a1-5207-a031-4d811fa7f0dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449512} {:answer/id #uuid "b0e9a6dd-aa8d-53df-aa34-38929292da67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449513}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449512} :answer-field/id #uuid "abb845e0-0f31-593e-85f2-f6c94ef89a74" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450710}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a68d3690-fbcf-53d1-acbf-a5134efed5cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-132728" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2)?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(0,2)$

- **II.** ${f}_{x}(1,0)$ is defined

- **III.** ${f}_{y}(1,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(0,2)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡2,
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,2) & =\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=0 \\ {f}_{y}(0,2) & =\frac{2(2)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,0)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{0}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1)
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is also false. If we substitute $(1,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{1}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0)
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."} :step/id #uuid "574ad7f2-698f-50d6-8eee-36f6145d16e5"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "be072909-07f4-5637-903f-a70436d30a22" :answer/type $$

$$
\begin{aligned}y\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}.\end{aligned}

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(0,2)$

- **II.** ${f}_{x}(1,0)$ is defined

$$

$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,2) & =\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=0 \\ {f}_{y}(0,2) & =\frac{2(2)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,0)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{0}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1)
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

$$
f(1,0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{1}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0)
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(4,2)$

- **II.** ${f}_{x}(0,2)$ is defined

- **III.** ${f}_{y}(0,2)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{y}^{2}\sqrt{x}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot (-\frac{2}{{y}^{3}}) \\  & =-\frac{2\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(4,2)$, where we have 

$$
f(4,2)=\frac{\sqrt{4}}{{2}^{2}}=\frac{1}{2},
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(4,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(4,2) & =\frac{1}{2({2}^{2})\sqrt{4}}=\frac{1}{16} \\ {f}_{y}(4,2) & =-\frac{2\sqrt{4}}{{2}^{3}}=-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(0,2)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,2)=\frac{1}{2({2}^{2})\sqrt{0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,2)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,2)=\frac{\sqrt{0}}{{2}^{2}}=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(0,2)=-\frac{2\sqrt{0}}{{2}^{3}}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only"."} :step/id #uuid "7b68aec1-f3e3-5aa1-bec7-f5fcbb362752" :step/next {:db/id 17592186445258}} {:db/id 17592186445261 :step/content {:db/id 17592186382221 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "45d1ed56-bfc6-5bda-a5c6-d5385ab5bd77" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453940} {:answer/id #uuid "bf41f840-b49c-5384-a274-dfe536fcb33d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453941}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453941} :answer-field/id #uuid "edafd0ac-42e0-5d4a-be7b-7aa902ffa1b6" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454720} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "060c118c-98d6-5841-94fb-d05d803c937b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453942} {:answer/id #uuid "3ca503bc-9f0b-57b9-9107-116d82172e36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453943}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453942} :answer-field/id #uuid "97a453da-0bfb-5722-95ac-96c9ea20e34e" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454721} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4b8b8bc4-d09b-5051-b032-eb64e490a6af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453944} {:answer/id #uuid "5922a222-d689-5f69-94af-6d12b904bec7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453945}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453944} :answer-field/id #uuid "5e81b99c-60a0-5dd3-8161-a53cd384fae9" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454722}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "ff98942c-b72f-558c-86fd-786f6575a16d" :question/math-academy-id "q-72019" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2x+y-z}?$

- **II.** ${f}_{z}(0,1,2)$ is defined

- **III.** The partial derivative with respect to $x$ is defined at $(0,1,1)$" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x}$ is defined only when $x\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{y}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{z}$ is defined only when $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(4,2):$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
f(0,2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡2,
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,2) & =\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=0 \\ {f}_{y}(0,2) & =\frac{2(2)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,0)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{0}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1)
$$

- Statement III is also false. If we substitute $(1,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{1}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0)
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
f(0,1,2)=\sqrt{2\cdot 0+1-2}=\sqrt{-1},
$$

which is undefined since the number under the radical is negative.

$$
{f}_{x}(0,1,1)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot 0+1-1}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-132675" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The partial derivative with respect to $y$ is defined at $(-1,-1,0)$
- **II.** ${f}_{x}(0,1,1)$ is defined
- **III.** ${f}_{z}(1,-1,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{z}{x} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{z}{y} \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(z) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(-1,-1,0)$, where we have 

$$
f(-1,-1,0)=0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡((-1)\cdot (-1))=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(-1,-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,-1,0) & =\frac{0}{(-1)}=0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(0,1,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,1,1)=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

- Statement III is also false. If we substitute $(1,-1,1)$ into ${f}_{z}$, we get

$$
{f}_{z}(1,-1,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot (-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1),
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."} :step/id #uuid "60152d46-a564-5e18-b836-e8be243798bf"} {:db/id 17592186494017 :step/content {:db/id 17592186426720 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9a414987-4111-5550-9b84-35b48e518248" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0,\,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z" :db/id 17592186426709} {:answer/id #uuid "c4574d37-c2e2-5922-8956-3143f5bef26f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y>0,\,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186426712} {:answer/id #uuid "c67ec9fa-9f76-59b9-b6ed-a85557705824" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y>0,\,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z" :db/id 17592186426713} {:answer/id #uuid "ee7e5c9b-05ac-5232-9af8-bc55f1d66335" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,\,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186426715} {:answer/id #uuid "f480f4b0-b440-57d3-be41-894b18986911" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,\,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z" :db/id 17592186426716}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426716} :answer-field/id #uuid "4d0f4a07-8c58-5c53-b0aa-71dedf0ab601" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186426719}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "13585dd1-9ab5-5887-870c-2d899c40d4a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-132652" :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{y{sin}^{2}⁡z}
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "79e002bf-37b0-5c5a-a563-f450eae54650" :step/next {:db/id 17592186494007}} {:db/id 17592186494025 :step/content {:db/id 17592186493937 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "084ca7fb-683b-515d-bd79-6b47f18630b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186493404} {:answer/id #uuid "1352f5a0-9197-5682-a147-c4c731774502" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186493425} {:answer/id #uuid "6a0ef88e-c7ac-5cdc-ae0e-1efc196b01b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186493549} {:answer/id #uuid "82a72c3b-2c62-5d09-a02a-39b20b9aa673" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186493599} {:answer/id #uuid "d3bc4946-5ae0-59ab-8397-c509f69337df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186493726}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493549} :answer-field/id #uuid "8c27c81b-25fa-5185-a05b-37e0f78454cf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493847}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "970e7795-a408-5210-80aa-25f375509b0b" :question/math-academy-id "q-65263" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}?$

I. The partial derivative with respect to $x$ is defined at $(1,-1,-1)$

II. ${f}_{y}(-1,1,1)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{z}(1,1,0)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{yz}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{yz{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{xz}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{xz{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{xy}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{xy{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,-1,-1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,-1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{1}}=e,
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-1,-1) & =\frac{(-1)(-1){e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}}{2\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1}}}{2\sqrt{1}}=\frac{e}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(-1,1,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(-1,1,1)={e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(1)(1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{-1}},
$$

which is undefined since we have a negative number under the radical. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(1,1,0)$ into ${f}_{z}$, we get

$$
{f}_{z}(1,1,0)=\frac{1\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}}{2\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I  only'."} :step/id #uuid "7f1dcee5-fe50-54b8-9541-d95743760a08" :step/next {:db/id 17592186494031}} {:db/id 17592186494031 :step/content {:db/id 17592186268903 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1e9af209-8790-5051-b760-8a2b7ab58c1e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1\}" :db/id 17592186493443} {:answer/id #uuid "2ae2e06a-4a60-5d0a-89f7-a1206ad8886c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186493462} {:answer/id #uuid "4da31340-f280-5ea2-b625-950af86420b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1\}" :db/id 17592186493517} {:answer/id #uuid "ee12a67f-64f9-5a94-956a-3d8cefbc2906" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0,\,z>0\}" :db/id 17592186493770} {:answer/id #uuid "f1099e4d-5739-5e2b-abdc-97a47dbd0d32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186493778}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493462} :answer-field/id #uuid "544bcd11-f607-53b0-99d1-1273ed387e89" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268559}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f03ff15b-864a-54f0-95c4-85eaad4622ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-132650" :question/problem "Given that $g(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{z}$ and

$$
\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{2y}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)},\,\frac{∂g}{∂z}=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{{z}^{2}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $g$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $g(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{z}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is 

$$
{D}_{g}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${g}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{2x}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1\ne 0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domain of ${g}_{y}(x,y,z)$ is the same: 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{y}}={D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function ${g}_{z}(x,y,z)=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{{z}^{2}}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{z}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{z}} & ={D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{z}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & \,\,\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & \,\,\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "87fc833d-38e2-5311-a2c8-c3e5fcb40ab1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186494017}} {:db/id 17592186494068 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124995 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b903ce0b-98c6-57d8-9e48-735e14bb633f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186448584} {:answer/id #uuid "e89b1128-0cdb-5f83-9979-822275c3412d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186448585}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186448585} :answer-field/id #uuid "62e75cd6-e230-5ef5-921b-7e8382a039af" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186449332} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b15a164-a197-53c5-b168-a0a97d0c6836" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186448586} {:answer/id #uuid "c7106db2-aab9-5e51-b215-01c8b91bedc9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186448587}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186448586} :answer-field/id #uuid "028cafa1-ca77-5fce-9098-ff08007d68ae" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186449333} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a0b2a1b1-098a-5a44-83b4-193b393fe615" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186448588} {:answer/id #uuid "5b241cba-015b-566d-8a54-d752edb0b3b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186448589}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186448588} :answer-field/id #uuid "17e7993b-564d-5df7-9cb5-369c37279a0f" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186449334}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cee8f940-b17d-518d-bf59-666639ac6929" :question/math-academy-id "q-36504" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y})?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,1)$
- **II.** ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is defined
- **III.** ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that $f$ is defined only when

$$
\frac{x}{x+y}>0.
$$

At points in the domain of $f,$ we can compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{1\cdot (x+y)-x\cdot 1}{(x+y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{y}{(x+y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{y}{x(x+y)} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{x}{(x+y)^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. The function is defined at $(1,1),$ since

$$
f(1,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{1+1})=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}),
$$

and both partial derivatives are defined there:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =\frac{1}{1(1+1)}=\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =-\frac{1}{1+1}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. At $(0,1),$

$$
\frac{x}{x+y}=\frac{0}{0+1}=0,
$$

so

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0),
$$

which is undefined. Therefore, ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is not defined.

- Statement III is false for the same reason. Since $f$ is not defined at $(0,1),$ the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is not defined. The simplified expression $-\frac{1}{x+y}$ cannot be used to define the partial derivative at a point outside the domain of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} :step/id #uuid "f230ec9a-d682-55d8-adbb-af178ec09394" :step/next {:db/id 17592186494025}}] :activity/title "Partial Differentiability of Multivariable 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cee8f940-b17d-518d-bf59-666639ac6929" :question/math-academy-id "q-36504" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y})?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,1)$
- **II.** ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is defined
- **III.** ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that $f$ is defined only when

$$
\frac{x}{x+y}>0.
$$

At points in the domain of $f,$ we can compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{1\cdot (x+y)-x\cdot 1}{(x+y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{y}{(x+y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{y}{x(x+y)} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{x}{(x+y)^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. The function is defined at $(1,1),$ since

$$
f(1,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{1+1})=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}),
$$

and both partial derivatives are defined there:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =\frac{1}{1(1+1)}=\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =-\frac{1}{1+1}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. At $(0,1),$

$$
\frac{x}{x+y}=\frac{0}{0+1}=0,
$$

so

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0),
$$

which is undefined. Therefore, ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is not defined.

- Statement III is false for the same reason. Since $f$ is not defined at $(0,1),$ the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is not defined. The simplified expression $-\frac{1}{x+y}$ cannot be used to define the partial derivative at a point outside the domain of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} :step/id #uuid "f230ec9a-d682-55d8-adbb-af178ec09394" :step/next {:db/id 17592186494025}} {:db/id 17592186494007 :step/content {:db/id 17592186268906 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8e430633-0c79-5bd0-864a-cc54142526aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449496} {:answer/id #uuid "99da71ad-b733-50e9-9bc1-232efc6cef4b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449497}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449497} :answer-field/id #uuid "ad351a32-8420-5f40-bd4e-3a76a453aa9b" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450702} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3e1d2654-71e6-5045-abb7-876f75070a78" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449498} {:answer/id #uuid "9a1659ae-9585-5275-84c0-eb9540469367" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449499}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449498} :answer-field/id #uuid "f83c3b78-80d6-5799-ba6a-86046c4eb7a9" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450703} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b65c5da8-b876-59b5-b16a-4a0a833c5303" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449500} {:answer/id #uuid "c93dd213-5575-5cca-b228-64873eafdfe4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449501}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449500} :answer-field/id #uuid "db1f014c-1d1e-5df1-9579-1cb65d8ea1ac" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450704}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "72f1f14f-947a-5dd6-902d-418c94ea31fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-132675" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)?$

$$
f(-1,-1,0)=0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡((-1)\cdot (-1))=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(-1,-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,-1,0) & =\frac{0}{(-1)}=0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(0,1,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,1,1)=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

- Statement III is also false. If we substitute $(1,-1,1)$ into ${f}_{z}$, we get

$$
{f}_{z}(1,-1,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot (-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1),
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$

{:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "13585dd1-9ab5-5887-870c-2d899c40d4a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-132652" :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{y{sin}^{2}⁡z}
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "79e002bf-37b0-5c5a-a563-f450eae54650" :step/next {:db/id 17592186494007}} {:db/id 17592186494025 :step/content {:db/id 17592186493937 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "084ca7fb-683b-515d-bd79-6b47f18630b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186493404} {:answer/id #uuid "1352f5a0-9197-5682-a147-c4c731774502" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186493425} {:answer/id #uuid "6a0ef88e-c7ac-5cdc-ae0e-1efc196b01b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186493549} {:answer/id #uuid "82a72c3b-2c62-5d09-a02a-39b20b9aa673" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186493599} {:answer/id #uuid "d3bc4946-5ae0-59ab-8397-c509f69337df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186493726}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493549} :answer-field/id #uuid "8c27c81b-25fa-5185-a05b-37e0f78454cf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493847}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "970e7795-a408-5210-80aa-25f375509b0b" :question/math-academy-id "q-65263" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}?$

I. The partial derivative with respect to $x$ is defined at $(1,-1,-1)$

II. ${f}_{y}(-1,1,1)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{z}(1,1,0)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{yz}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{yz{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{xz}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{xz{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{xy}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{xy{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,-1,-1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,-1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{1}}=e,
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-1,-1) & =\frac{(-1)(-1){e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}}{2\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1}}}{2\sqrt{1}}=\frac{e}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(-1,1,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(-1,1,1)={e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(1)(1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{-1}},
$$

which is undefined since we have a negative number under the radical. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(1,1,0)$ into ${f}_{z}$, we get

$$
{f}_{z}(1,1,0)=\frac{1\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}}{2\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I  only'."} :step/id #uuid "7f1dcee5-fe50-54b8-9541-d95743760a08" :step/next {:db/id 17592186494031}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid $g(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{z}$ and

$$
\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{2y}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)},\,\frac{∂g}{∂z}=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{{z}^{2}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $g$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $g(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{z}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is 

$$
{D}_{g}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${g}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{2x}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1\ne 0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domain of ${g}_{y}(x,y,z)$ is the same: 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{y}}={D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function ${g}_{z}(x,y,z)=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{{z}^{2}}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{z}$ is

{{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}\cdot {7}^{2x}-50\cdot {7}^{2x} & =0 \\ (2{x}^{2}-50)\cdot {7}^{2x} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can now apply the zero product property, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0.$ This gives us two equations,

$$
2{x}^{2}-50=0\,\text{and}\,{7}^{2x}=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- The equation $2{x}^{2}-50=0$ can be factored as

$$
\begin{aligned}2({x}^{2}-25) & =0 \\ 2(x-5)(x+5) & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which leads to the solutions $x=-5,5.$

- The equation $2=0$ is not a possible solution because it's a false statement.

- The equation ${7}^{2x}=0$ has no solutions because ${7}^{2x}$ is positive for every real number $x.$

Therefore, in ascending order, the original equation has the solutions

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot {5}^{x-2} & ={x}^{2}\cdot {5}^{x-2} \\ 4\cdot {5}^{x-2}-{x}^{2}\cdot {5}^{x-2} & =0 \\ (4-{x}^{2}){5}^{x-2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
4-{x}^{2}=0\,\text{and}\,{5}^{x-2}=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- The equation $4-{x}^{2}=0$ can be factored as

$$
(2+x)(2-x)=0,
$$

which leads to the solutions $x=-2,2.$

- The equation ${5}^{x-2}=0$ has no solutions because ${5}^{x-2}$ is positive for every real number $x.$
